A plan that discusses generator coverage at water plants and shelters, redundancy of feeds, and fuel resupply is engaging with the real problem; a bare facility list with no hazard overlay is checkbox compliance, and noticing the difference calibrates your trust in the rest of the document.

There is also a quiet privacy-shaped gap to be aware of. Some infrastructure detail, especially concerning dams, utilities, and security-sensitive sites, is summarized vaguely or held in non-public appendices, and plans will say so. If a facility that obviously matters to your area seems absent, it may be withheld rather than overlooked. The public version still usually tells you enough: counts of exposed facilities per hazard, the jurisdictions they sit in, and the mitigation actions proposed for them, which is where this section connects forward to the strategy chapter and to the question of whether the identified weak points are actually being fixed.

sections.heading: The Mitigation Strategy: Goals, Alternatives, and What Actually Gets Funded
sections.body:
The mitigation strategy chapter is where analysis is supposed to become intention. It opens with goals and objectives, broad statements like protect life and property from flooding, or maintain continuity of critical services, and while the goals themselves are usually unobjectionable to the point of blandness, their ordering and specificity reveal priorities. The substance follows in the catalog of mitigation actions, and understanding the standard taxonomy helps you see what kind of strategy your county has chosen. FEMA groups actions into families: local plans and regulations, meaning code adoption, zoning, floodplain and stormwater ordinances, and land-use steering; structure and infrastructure projects, meaning elevations, acquisitions and demolitions, retrofits, safe rooms, culvert and drainage upsizing, utility hardening, and seismic bracing; natural systems protection, meaning wetland restoration, floodplain reconnection, fuel management, and green stormwater infrastructure; and education and awareness programs, meaning outreach campaigns, workshops, and warning-system publicity. Some plans add preparedness and response support actions like generators and warning sirens, which sit at the boundary of mitigation proper.

The mix among these families is the strategy's real signature. Regulations and education are inexpensive and appear in every plan; hard projects cost real money and mark seriousness; natural-systems actions mark sophistication. A strategy of twenty actions of which eighteen are continue public outreach and support existing programs is a plan preserving grant eligibility while committing to little. A strategy that names specific projects, elevate or acquire the twelve repetitive-loss structures on Miller Creek, replace the Fourth Street culvert to pass the one-percent flow, construct a FEMA P-361 safe room at the fairgrounds, retrofit the water plant's electrical service above the five-hundred-year elevation, is a plan that did its homework and intends to spend. The linkage test from earlier applies with full force here: set the action list beside the risk assessment's top-ranked hazards and highest loss estimates and see whether they correspond.

It helps to know how projects move from these tables into reality, because the plan is the first link in a funding chain. When a disaster is declared, HMGP money becomes available statewide and communities submit applications drawn, ideally, from their plan's action list; nationally competitive BRIC and flood-specific FMA cycles run on annual calendars. Applications must pass benefit-cost analysis, demonstrating that expected avoided losses exceed project cost using FEMA's methodology, which is why actions in the plan sometimes carry preliminary cost estimates and benefit narratives. Projects also need a non-federal cost share, typically twenty-five percent, and a capable applicant to manage them, which is where the capability assessment's honesty matters. A county with one part-time emergency manager cannot execute ten simultaneous federal grants, and realistic plans scale their ambitions accordingly or lean on state agencies and regional councils for administration.

As a reader, extract three practical things from the strategy chapter. First, what is planned near you: a drainage project on your street, a buyout program in your neighborhood, a fuel break above your subdivision. Second, what the county believes it cannot do, which appears between the lines as absent action types or explicit statements about staffing and fiscal constraints. Third, where citizen pressure would be productive: actions listed but unfunded are the shovel-ready candidates the next disaster's HMGP money could fund, and elected officials respond to residents who ask about specific plan actions by name and number.

sections.heading: Reading the Action Tables: Priority, Cost, Lead Agency, and Status
sections.body:
The action tables are the plan's most operational pages, usually formatted as a grid with one row per action and columns for an identifier, a description, the hazards addressed, the jurisdiction, a lead agency, potential funding sources, an estimated cost, a priority rating, and a target timeframe. Update plans add the most diagnostic column of all: the status of each action carried over from the previous cycle, marked completed, in progress, ongoing, deferred, or deleted. Learning to read these grids critically takes ten minutes and converts you from a passive reader into someone who can hold the process accountable.

Start with the status column in an updated plan, because it is the report card on the last five years. Count the completions. A county that completed even a handful of hard projects, a culvert replaced, a set of acquisitions closed, a safe room built, a station generator installed, has a functioning mitigation program. A table where every prior action reappears as ongoing or deferred, cycle after cycle, documents a program that exists on paper. Be fair in the counting: ongoing is a legitimate status for genuinely continuous actions like enforcing the floodplain ordinance or maintaining CRS participation, so distinguish perpetual-by-nature actions from stalled projects wearing the same label. Some plans include a narrative implementation review alongside the table; where it exists it often explains the honest reasons, a failed grant application, a landowner who declined a buyout, a cost estimate that doubled.

Next, interrogate the priority ratings and how they were assigned. Many plans document a scoring method, and a common one is the STAPLEE framework, which weighs each action's social acceptability, technical feasibility, administrative capacity, political support, legal authority, economic justification, and environmental soundness; others use simple high, medium, low judgments by the planning committee, and newer guidance emphasizes cost-effectiveness and equity considerations. The method matters less than consistency, and the useful trick is to look for mismatches: a high-priority rating on an action with no identified funding source and a distant timeframe is an aspiration; a medium-priority action with a named lead, a named grant program, and a two-year window is the one that will actually happen. The lead agency column deserves similar scrutiny, because an action assigned to everyone is assigned to no one; the strongest entries name a specific department and even a position.

Cost columns are order-of-magnitude estimates and should be read as such; the informative comparison is internal, seeing which actions the county considers cheap enough to self-fund versus dependent on federal grants, since the funding-source column stating HMGP, BRIC, or FMA implicitly tells you the action waits on a grant cycle or a disaster declaration. Timeframes labeled short, medium, and long are defined somewhere in the chapter, commonly one to two, three to five, and beyond five years; check the definitions rather than assuming. Finally, find your own jurisdiction's rows in a multi-jurisdictional plan, because the county-level table often differs from your city's annex, and it is the annex that governs what your own government promised. Write down the identifiers of the two or three actions nearest your home or your concerns; those numbers are the handle you will use at public meetings, in emails to officials, and when the next update's comment period opens.

sections.heading: Using the Plan for Your Own Address and Household Decisions
sections.body:
The county wrote its plan to manage community risk, but a careful resident can mine it for a personal risk assessment that would cost real money to commission privately. The method is to walk the plan's own structure at the scale of your address: which profiled hazards touch my parcel, what does the mapped and historical record say about my immediate area, which nearby vulnerabilities would cascade to me, and which of the county's planned actions change my picture. An hour with the plan and a notepad typically produces a short, specific list of exposures, and each exposure suggests a decision about insurance, retrofit, or preparation.

Flood is the natural starting point because the mapping is best. Establish whether your building is in the SFHA, in the shaded 0.2-percent zone, or outside both, using the plan's maps as orientation and FEMA's Map Service Center for the authoritative current FIRM panel. Then apply the correction this guide keeps stressing: check the plan's flood history for chronic problem areas outside the mapped zones, because local drainage flooding is real risk the maps do not carry. The insurance implication runs one way only: flood damage is excluded from standard homeowners policies, and an NFIP or private flood policy is purchasable outside high-risk zones at modest cost, so discovering that your area appears in the plan's flood history while sitting outside the SFHA is an argument for buying coverage, not for relief. Note also the thirty-day waiting period on new NFIP policies, which forecloses buying protection when a storm is already on the map. If the plan shows dam inundation zones or unaccredited levees affecting your area, add those to the flood column of your notes; they represent low-probability, high-consequence scenarios that argue for knowing your evacuation route even if you never buy another dollar of coverage.

Wind, fire, and earthquake exposures translate into retrofit and behavior decisions. In hail and wind country, the plan's storm history informs roofing choices, impact-rated coverings, and whether a tornado safe room, which grant programs sometimes cost-share for homeowners, is worth pursuing; if you live in a manufactured home, the plan's shelter inventory tells you where the nearest community safe room is, and its absence tells you to identify a sturdy alternative now. In WUI areas, the mapped severity zones and any named fuel-reduction priority areas indicate how aggressively to pursue defensible space, ember-resistant vents, and Class A roofing, and whether a local chipping or cost-share program exists to help. In seismic areas, the profile's discussion of building eras and soil conditions frames the classic questions of bolting the frame to the foundation, bracing cripple walls, and strapping the water heater.

Finally, use the critical-facilities analysis to reality-test your household plan. If the plan shows your water system, your access bridge, or your designated shelter as exposed, extend your self-sufficiency assumptions accordingly: more stored water, a longer outage horizon, an alternate route, a different shelter destination. And put one date in your calendar: the plan's next update cycle. The document you have been reading is revised every five years with a public comment period, and the difference between a resident who reads the plan and one who shows up to comment on it is the difference between using the process and improving it.

sections.heading: The Planning Process Chapter: Who Was at the Table and Why It Matters
sections.body:
The planning process chapter reads like administrative throat-clearing, meeting dates, invitation lists, sign-in sheets, and most readers skip it. Skim it anyway, because federal regulation makes process a condition of approval for a reason: the plan's content is downstream of who shaped it, and this chapter is where you find out. The regulation requires an open public involvement process with opportunity for the public to comment during drafting and before approval, participation opportunities for neighboring communities, agencies, businesses, academia, and other interests, and review of existing plans and studies. The chapter documents compliance, and in doing so it inadvertently documents the plan's blind spots.

Read the participant roster with three questions. First, was participation broad or thin? A planning team of one emergency manager and a hired consultant produces a different document than a team that included public works, planning and zoning, the floodplain administrator, school and hospital representatives, utility operators, fire districts, and social service agencies. Each absent perspective predicts a weak section: no utility at the table often means a shallow infrastructure analysis, no social services often means vulnerable populations handled in a paragraph of census numbers. Second, in multi-jurisdictional plans, did each jurisdiction genuinely participate? The regulation requires each to do so in order to adopt the plan and gain eligibility, and the chapter's participation table shows who attended what; a town whose entire involvement was one email appears in the record, and its annex will usually read as thin as its engagement. Third, how was the public actually engaged? The floor is a legal notice and a hearing nobody attends; the ceiling is a real survey with hundreds of responses, open houses in multiple towns, and documented changes made in response to comments. Plans often reproduce survey results in an appendix, and they are worth a look in their own right, because they show what your neighbors fear most, which sometimes diverges sharply from the technical ranking, residents rating winter storms above the floods that dominate the loss statistics, or vice versa; the divergence between perceived and modeled risk is where public outreach actions in the strategy chapter come from.

The chapter also lists the studies and plans reviewed during drafting, and this bibliography is a resource in itself: the county's comprehensive plan, stormwater studies, dam emergency action plans, the state hazard mitigation plan, watershed studies, and prior disaster after-action reports. If you want to go deeper on any hazard than the mitigation plan itself goes, this list is your reading map, and the state plan in particular, a much larger document maintained by the state emergency management agency, contains regional analysis that contextualizes your county's numbers.

There is a practical payoff to knowing the process as well. The chapter names the plan's custodian, the standing committee or position responsible for maintenance, and describes how mid-cycle input is received. That is the address for your questions and, when the update cycle begins, your comments. Counties genuinely struggle to get public participation in mitigation planning, to the point that documented turnout is a compliance headache; a resident who arrives having read the current plan, referencing specific actions by number and specific gaps by section, is rare enough to be remembered and effective out of proportion to the effort involved.

sections.heading: Plan Maintenance, Five-Year Updates, and How to Get Involved
sections.body:
A mitigation plan is legally alive for five years from its federal approval, and the maintenance chapter describes how it is supposed to be kept alive in practice: an annual review by a standing committee, monitoring of action progress, evaluation after significant disasters, integration of the plan into other county mechanisms, and the procedure for the eventual full update. Reading this chapter last makes sense, because it tells you what happens next and where a resident fits into it.

The integration language deserves more attention than its dry phrasing invites. The regulation requires plans to describe how mitigation will be incorporated into other planning mechanisms, such as comprehensive plans, capital improvement budgets, and ordinances, and this is where mitigation either becomes real or does not. A flood mitigation goal achieves nothing by existing in a shelf document; it achieves something when the subdivision ordinance requires new lots to have buildable area above the base flood elevation, when the capital budget schedules the culvert replacement the plan proposed, when the comprehensive plan steers growth away from the mapped hazard areas the risk assessment identified. When you read the maintenance chapter's integration commitments, you are reading promises whose fulfillment you can check in entirely public places: zoning amendments, budget documents, council agendas. Post-disaster evaluation language matters too; after a declared disaster, the county updating its plan while applying for HMGP funds is the system working as designed, and the after-action lessons should surface in the next cycle's hazard profiles.

The five-year update is the main event, and its rhythm is predictable enough to plan around. Roughly a year to eighteen months before expiration, the county seeks funding, often a planning grant from the same federal programs, hires a consultant or assigns staff, and convenes the planning team. Data updates, hazard profile revisions, a new public survey, and jurisdiction meetings follow, then a public comment draft, state review, FEMA review, the approvable-pending-adoption status described earlier, adoption resolutions by every participating governing body, and final approval that restarts the clock. Public comment windows occur at minimum on the draft, and often at the front end through surveys and open houses. If you have read the current plan using this guide, you are equipped to comment usefully at either point: naming hazards the identification section screened out too casually, correcting local flood history from lived observation, which planners genuinely value because gauge records miss small drainages, questioning stalled actions by number, and advocating for specific projects in your area to be added, since presence in the plan is a precondition for later grant funding.

Between cycles, involvement is lower-effort and still worthwhile. Attend the annual review meeting if it is public, or ask the emergency management office for the annual progress report. Show up when a proposed development in a mapped hazard area comes before the planning commission, and cite the plan's own risk assessment; it is the county's document, and quoting it back is legitimate and surprisingly forceful. Ask your city council member whether the actions in your city's annex have lead agencies actually working on them. None of this requires expertise beyond what the plan itself has now given you. The document was paid for publicly, written to be approved, and too rarely read; a resident who reads it closes the loop the whole system quietly depends on.

guides.safetyNote: A hazard mitigation plan is a planning document, not a warning system, and reading one is never a substitute for acting on official watches, warnings, and evacuation orders from emergency management, the National Weather Service, or local authorities. If the plan leads you to investigate hazards around your home, treat the hazards themselves with respect: never walk or drive through floodwater, since six inches of moving water can knock an adult down and about a foot can float a car; stay clear of damaged structures, downed power lines, and post-fire slopes at risk of debris flow; and hire licensed professionals for structural retrofits, gas, and electrical work.

guides.title: Setting Realistic Preparedness Planning Horizons
guides.summary: How to decide how long a household should be able to sustain itself without outside supply, using real disruption durations rather than fear or fashion. Covers the standard tiers, the resource that limits each one, a procedure for setting your own horizon, and the maintenance burden that quietly destroys over-ambitious plans.

sections.heading: What a Planning Horizon Is and Why It Decides Everything Else
sections.body:
A planning horizon is the single number that answers the question: how long must this household be able to feed, water, warm, medicate and organise itself with no resupply from outside? Everything else in preparedness is downstream of it. The horizon determines how much water you store, whether food can be ordinary groceries or must be shelf-stable specialist stock, whether a torch and batteries suffice or you need a generator, whether a first-aid kit is enough or you need a month of prescriptions in hand. Choose the number first and the shopping list writes itself. Choose the shopping list first, which is what most people do, and you end up with a pile of equipment that does not correspond to any coherent scenario.

The horizon is also the thing that most often goes wrong, in both directions. Under-set, it produces households with a torch and half a case of bottled water facing a five-day outage in February. Over-set, it produces something worse in a quieter way: a plan so large that nobody maintains it. Buckets of wheat bought in 2016 and never opened, water containers that developed algae, a generator that will not start because it sat with untreated petrol in the carburettor for four years. An unmaintained one-year plan is frequently less useful in a real emergency than a maintained two-week one, because the two-week supply is rotated, familiar and actually edible.

The concept borrows deliberately from professional continuity planning, where the equivalent terms are the recovery time objective and the maximum tolerable period of disruption. Businesses do not ask how long a disaster might last in the abstract; they ask how long they can survive without a given function before harm becomes unacceptable, then build capability to bridge exactly that gap. Households benefit from the same discipline. The question is not "what is the worst thing that could happen" — an unbounded question with no useful answer — but "what is the longest plausible period during which normal supply is unavailable to me, here, given what actually happens in this place."

That last qualifier matters enormously. A household in the wildfire-urban interface of northern California, one on the Gulf Coast, one in an apartment in a Nordic city with district heating, and one on a rural single-track power line in the Scottish Highlands face profoundly different disruption profiles. Their horizons should differ by a factor of five or more. Generic advice cannot set the number for you; it can only supply the tiers, the evidence base, and the method. The horizon is the output of a short, honest analysis of local hazards, local infrastructure fragility, and your own household's tolerance, and it should be written down as a number, because a horizon that lives only as a vague intention to "be prepared" quietly becomes zero.

sections.heading: The Cost Curve: Why Each Extra Week Costs More Than the Last
sections.body:
Preparedness expenditure does not scale linearly with the horizon, and understanding why is the key to setting a sensible one. The first three days are extraordinarily cheap. Almost every household already owns most of what is needed: some food in the cupboard, taps that were full when the disruption began, a phone with a charge, blankets. Formalising a 72-hour capability typically costs the price of a few cases of water, a torch, a battery radio, a spare charging bank and some tinned goods — call it 60 to 150 units of currency for a family of four, most of it food that will be eaten anyway.

The second tier, out to roughly two weeks, still uses ordinary goods but requires deliberate storage. Water is the first thing to become awkward: two weeks for four people at the standard planning figure of about four litres per person per day is 224 litres, which is roughly five 45-litre drums or two hundred and twenty-four one-litre bottles, and it occupies real floor space and weighs 224 kilograms. Food remains supermarket food, just more of it and chosen for shelf life. Cost perhaps rises to several hundred.

Past a month the curve steepens sharply, because ordinary goods stop working. Bread, fresh milk, fresh produce and chilled meat all fail on shelf life, so the diet must shift to freeze-dried, retort-pouched, canned or dry-staple foods, which cost two to five times as much per calorie than the equivalent fresh diet, or demand grain-milling and cooking skills most households do not have. Water can no longer be stored in useful quantity — 90 days for four people is roughly 1,440 litres, more than a tonne — so the plan must become a treatment plan rather than a storage plan, which means filters, chemical disinfection, a rainwater or surface-water source and the competence to use them. Power for that duration means fuel logistics, not batteries. Medication means negotiating with a healthcare system that is generally not designed to dispense a quarter of a year at once.

Beyond a year, the plan is no longer preparedness at all; it is a change in mode of living. Sustaining a household for twelve months without resupply implies food production or a very large capital investment in stored calories, sanitation infrastructure independent of the sewer, and a security posture, because a year-long disruption of that severity implies a social environment quite unlike the one the plan was written in. That is a legitimate choice for some people in some places, but it should be made with eyes open, and it should not be smuggled in by increments.

The practical implication is that marginal return per unit of money and effort falls steadily while marginal cost rises. The steepest part of the benefit curve lies between zero and about fourteen days, which is precisely where most national civil-protection agencies now point, and where a household with limited budget and limited storage should concentrate almost all of its effort.

sections.heading: Grounding the Horizon in Real Hazard Data, Not Imagination
sections.body:
The horizon should be derived from the hazards that actually occur where you live, at the frequencies at which they occur, and this is knowable. Most countries publish a national risk assessment, and many regions publish local ones. The United Kingdom's National Risk Register, the United States' FEMA National Risk Index down to county level, Canada's public safety hazard profiles, Australia's state emergency service hazard maps and the European Union's member-state risk assessments all present hazards with rough likelihoods and consequence ranges. Local authorities and utilities publish outage statistics. Insurance flood maps show inundation extents by return period.

Working from these sources rather than from imagination changes the answer substantially. A household on a distribution circuit that has suffered three multi-day winter outages in ten years has strong empirical grounds for a fourteen-day power-independent horizon. A household in a dense city with underground cabling, three independent feeds and a documented mean outage duration of 40 minutes has grounds for a much shorter power horizon and should probably spend its effort on earthquake or heat instead. Neither household learns this from a general preparedness book.

The useful analytical frame is to separate hazards by return period and by duration, then take the envelope. Something with a one-in-five-year return period is nearly certain within a normal adult lifetime and should be planned for fully; something with a one-in-five-hundred-year return period may still deserve attention if its consequence is catastrophic and the mitigation is cheap, but it should not set the household horizon. Between the two lies the pragmatic band, roughly the one-in-ten to one-in-hundred-year events, which is what most professional planning targets.

Two systematic biases distort this badly if left unchecked. The first is availability bias: the most recent or most vividly reported disaster dominates attention regardless of its relevance. After a widely televised hurricane, inland households buy hurricane supplies. After a pandemic, everyone buys masks and nobody buys a water filter. The corrective is to write the hazard list from documented local data before consulting memory or news. The second is the tendency to plan for the exciting hazard rather than the likely one. Statistically the disruptions that actually strip a household of services are, in most of the developed world and in this rough order: severe weather causing extended power loss, flooding, winter storms, wildfire evacuation, and localised infrastructure failure such as a water main contamination or gas outage. Structural collapse of society appears in the imagination far more often than in the record.

A last grounding step is to check the failure modes of your own specific infrastructure. Does your water supply require electric pumping, so that a power cut is also a water cut? Is your heating gas, electric, or district? Does your building's fire and lift system fail safe? Do you live above the fifth floor, where an outage means carrying every litre of water up the stairs by hand? These local details often move the horizon more than the hazard category does.

sections.heading: The Standard Tiers and What Each One Actually Buys
sections.body:
Preparedness guidance across the world has converged, largely independently, on a small number of tiers, and it is worth understanding what each is designed to bridge rather than treating them as arbitrary round numbers.

The 72-hour tier is the oldest and most widely promoted. Its logic is response-time based: it is roughly how long organised outside assistance takes to reach a disaster area at scale, and it is the figure behind the American Ready.gov campaign, Japan's long-standing bousai guidance and many Red Cross programmes. Three days covers a typical storm outage, a short evacuation, or the gap before shelters and distribution points open. It is genuinely achievable for almost every household and remains the minimum defensible standard.

The one-to-two-week tier has grown steadily since the 2010s as evidence accumulated that 72 hours was optimistic. Ready.gov now recommends two weeks of water where storage permits. The German BBK advises ten days of food and drink. Switzerland's federal guidance is one week. Finland's 72 hours campaign explicitly acknowledges longer scenarios. New Zealand moved to seven days after the Canterbury earthquakes. The evidence driving this shift is straightforward: the 2021 Texas winter storm left some households without water for over a week; Hurricane Maria left much of Puerto Rico without grid power for months, with the median restoration measured in weeks; the 2003 Northeast blackout was short but the 1998 North American ice storm left parts of Quebec dark for over thirty days. Two weeks is the tier that survives contact with the historical record for most temperate-zone hazards.

The one-to-three-month tier is where planning changes character. Its usual justification is not a single disruption but a compound one — an economic shock, prolonged unemployment, a supply-chain interruption, a quarantine, or a regional disaster with slow recovery. In practice most households that achieve this tier do so partly for financial resilience rather than physical isolation: a well-stocked pantry is a hedge against a lost job as much as against a storm. This tier is realistic for a household with storage space, and it demands rotation discipline and a diet built from shelf-stable staples.

The one-year-plus tier is a lifestyle. It is the historical norm for agrarian households and the explicit teaching of some religious communities, notably the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, whose long-standing home storage guidance has produced a large body of practical knowledge on the subject. It requires a substantial capital outlay, dedicated dry, dark, cool storage, water independence rather than water storage, and continuing effort measured in hours per month.

The right answer for most households in a functioning state is to be genuinely excellent at two weeks and to extend towards three months in the specific commodities that are cheap and durable, chiefly food staples and fuel, rather than to reach uniformly for a longer horizon across every category at once.

sections.heading: Duration Against Severity: The Two Axes People Confuse
sections.body:
A great deal of muddled preparedness comes from collapsing two independent variables into one. Duration is how long the disruption lasts. Severity is how much of normal function it removes. They vary independently, and a plan built for one will not cover the other.

A three-hour total loss of all services is high severity, low duration, and essentially harmless to a prepared household. A three-month loss of a single service — say, potable tap water while electricity, gas, roads and shops all continue — is low severity, long duration, and requires a completely different response, mostly bottled water purchasing and a filter, with no need for a generator or food stores at all. This exact scenario has occurred repeatedly, for instance in numerous boil-water notices lasting weeks and in the Flint, Michigan water crisis, where the failure was quality rather than quantity and persisted for years.

The productive approach is to build the plan service by service, giving each its own horizon, rather than assuming everything fails together for the same period. A household might reasonably conclude: power, fourteen days; water, seven days stored plus indefinite treatment capability; heating, ten days at reduced comfort in one room; food, thirty days; medication, thirty days; cash, fourteen days of essential spending; communications, seven days. These are different numbers because the underlying systems have different fragilities and different restoration times, and the resources required to bridge them differ wildly in cost. Water for seven days is heavy but cheap; medication for thirty days may be administratively impossible; food for thirty days is easy and cheap.

Severity also determines whether shelter-in-place or evacuation is the correct mode, and this is a genuine branch point that many household plans omit entirely. A wildfire, a chemical release, a dam failure, or a structural threat calls for leaving quickly with a small kit and does not benefit from a large stored pantry at all — the pantry burns. An ice storm, a pandemic, a grid failure, or a civil disruption calls for staying put with a large pantry and no need to travel. A household that has only prepared to shelter is helpless in an evacuation and vice versa, so the honest plan carries both: a modest grab bag sized for hours to days, and a home supply sized for the shelter horizon.

The final confusion worth naming is between disruption of supply and disruption of income. These feel similar and demand different responses. A six-month income loss does not stop the shops working; it stops you buying from them. The preparedness response is savings, reduced fixed costs, a deep pantry of cheap staples and an understanding of local food assistance, not a generator. For most households in most decades, income disruption is by a wide margin the likeliest severe disruption they will ever experience, and it deserves at least as much planning attention as the weather.

sections.heading: How Long Real Disruptions Actually Last: The Evidence Base
sections.body:
Setting a horizon well requires knowing the empirical distribution of disruption durations rather than guessing. The record is patchy but informative, and its consistent lesson is that the distribution has a long tail: most events are short, a meaningful minority are far longer than planners expect, and the tail is where households get hurt.

For electricity in developed grids, routine reliability is high. The standard measure, SAIDI, the system average interruption duration index, runs around 60 to 120 minutes per customer per year in much of western Europe, higher in the United States at roughly 3 to 8 hours excluding major events, and considerably higher once major events are included. But these averages describe the ordinary case. Major-event durations are what matter. The January 1998 North American ice storm left some Quebec customers without power for more than five weeks. Hurricane Maria in 2017 left Puerto Rico with the longest blackout in modern United States history, with full restoration taking roughly eleven months and the median customer waiting weeks to months. Hurricane Ida in 2021 left parts of Louisiana dark for two to three weeks in extreme heat. The February 2021 Texas event, Winter Storm Uri, was shorter in raw outage terms, typically one to four days, but it simultaneously froze water systems, so millions were under boil-water notices for a week or more and hundreds of deaths followed.

Water disruptions display a similar shape. Boil-water advisories usually resolve in one to three days, but multi-week events after flooding are routine, and contamination events can run for months. In the 2007 Gloucestershire floods in England, around 350,000 people lost mains water for up to seventeen days and were supplied by bowsers and bottled distribution.

Supply-chain and economic disruptions run longer and shallower. The 2020 to 2022 period demonstrated that specific goods can vanish from shelves for weeks while overall supply continues, and that logistics recovery is measured in months. Fuel disruptions, such as the 2021 Colonial Pipeline shutdown and the United Kingdom fuel crises of 2000 and 2021, produced acute local shortages lasting roughly five to fourteen days, largely driven by panic buying rather than physical shortfall.

Evacuations are shorter in the acute phase and much longer in the return phase. Most wildfire evacuations release residents within three to ten days, but a destroyed home means displacement measured in months to years, which is a housing and insurance problem rather than a supplies problem.

Reading across all of this, a defensible generalisation is that a fourteen-day horizon covers the great majority of service disruptions in a functioning state, that a thirty-day food horizon costs little and covers most of the remainder, and that events lasting beyond a few months are qualitatively different, involving displacement, institutional collapse or economic hardship rather than simply a longer version of the same problem. Planning to fourteen days thoroughly beats planning to a year carelessly.

sections.heading: A Procedure for Setting Your Own Horizon
sections.body:
The following procedure produces a written, defensible horizon in about two hours of work, and its output is a short document rather than a purchase. Do the analysis before spending money; the ordering matters, because equipment bought before the analysis tends to determine the plan rather than serve it.

The result should be a single page listing each essential service, its horizon in days, the constraint that sets that number, and the current gap. Revisit it annually, and immediately after any move, birth, diagnosis or change of heating system, since all of those shift the numbers materially.
steps: List every service your household depends on daily: electricity, drinking water, sanitation, heating or cooling, cooking, food supply, medication, refrigeration for medicines, communications, transport, money access, and any care dependency such as a powered medical device or a family member who cannot be left alone.

For each service, write down what physically supplies it and what that supply itself depends on. Note in particular any hidden electrical dependency: mains water is often electrically pumped, gas boilers need mains power for controls and pumps, and many sanitation systems rely on electric lift pumps.

Pull your local hazard profile from an official source — a national risk register, a county-level risk index, your utility's published outage history, and the local flood map — and list the hazards with roughly a one-in-ten to one-in-hundred-year return period in your specific location.

For each hazard, write the plausible duration range it imposes on each service, using documented past events in your region rather than estimates. Where local data is absent, use the nearest comparable event elsewhere and say so.

Take the ninetieth-percentile duration across your realistic hazards for each service separately. That number, rounded up to a whole number of days, is that service's provisional horizon. Do not use a single horizon across all services.

Apply a household vulnerability adjustment. Add days for an infant, a person needing refrigerated medication, limited mobility, an upper-floor flat with no lift, a rural location with a single access road, or no vehicle. Subtract days only if you have a genuinely reliable fallback such as a nearby relative outside the hazard zone with a written agreement, not merely an assumption.

Sanity-check each horizon against your storage space, budget and rotation capacity. A horizon you cannot store, afford, and rotate is not a horizon, it is a wish. Reduce it and record the shortfall honestly rather than pretending.

Convert each horizon into a quantity: litres of water, days of calories, kilowatt-hours or fuel litres, doses of medication, currency in small notes. Compare against what you already hold and write the gap.
Decide the shelter-or-leave branch for each hazard and size a separate grab bag for the evacuation cases, typically 24 to 72 hours of essentials that one person can carry.
Write the single page, date it, put a copy somewhere accessible without power, and set a calendar reminder to review it in twelve months.

sections.heading: Water: The Constraint That Bites First and Hardest
sections.body:
Water sets the shortest hard deadline in any preparedness plan and is the resource most often underestimated. A person deprived of all fluid typically deteriorates severely within two to three days and dies within roughly three to seven depending on temperature and exertion, against three weeks or more for food. Any horizon beyond about 48 hours is therefore a water plan first and everything else second.

The standard planning figure is roughly 4 litres per person per day, split as about 2 to 3 litres for drinking and the remainder for basic food preparation and minimal hygiene. This figure is deliberately austere. It does not cover washing, laundry, or flushing. In heat, at altitude, during heavy exertion, or for a nursing mother, drinking requirements alone can reach 4 to 6 litres per day, and the Sphere humanitarian standards used in refugee contexts specify 15 litres per person per day as the minimum for full basic needs including hygiene. A household planning a comfortable rather than survivable fortnight should think in terms of 10 to 15 litres per person per day, which quickly becomes unstorable.

That collision is the reason water planning splits at roughly the one-week mark. Below a week, storage is the answer. Four people for seven days at 4 litres each is 112 litres, achievable in two 60-litre drums or a stack of commercial bottled water, weighing 112 kilograms and occupying under half a cubic metre. Above a week, storage becomes impractical for most homes and the plan must shift to treatment: a means of rendering a nearby source safe indefinitely. Sources include rainwater from a clean catchment, a stream or pond, a swimming pool for washing though not drinking, a water heater tank which typically holds 100 to 250 litres of potable water accessible via its drain valve, and the toilet cistern though not the bowl.

Treatment has three independent stages and confusion between them is a common and dangerous error. Filtration removes particles and, with a fine enough element, bacteria and protozoa including Cryptosporidium and Giardia; hollow-fibre filters rated to 0.1 or 0.2 micrometres do this reliably. Disinfection kills organisms chemically or thermally; boiling at a rolling boil for one minute, or three minutes above 2,000 metres altitude, is the most reliable method and inactivates viruses that many filters do not. Chemical disinfection with unscented household bleach at roughly 5 to 6 per cent sodium hypochlorite uses about two drops per litre of clear water, doubled for cloudy water, with a thirty-minute contact time and a faint chlorine smell as the confirmation. Neither filtration nor disinfection removes dissolved chemical contamination, heavy metals or salt; only distillation or reverse osmosis addresses those, and in a chemically contaminated event no household filter should be trusted.

Stored water should be rotated every six to twelve months if in reused containers, and commercially sealed bottled water remains safe well beyond its printed date if stored cool and dark, though the plastic may impart taste.

sections.heading: Food: Calories, Shelf Life, and the Diet That Matches the Horizon
sections.body:
Food is the most forgiving element of a preparedness plan and consequently the one where households most often over-invest in the wrong direction, buying specialist long-life products before they have a functioning ordinary pantry.

The physiological baseline is roughly 2,000 to 2,500 kilocalories per adult per day for normal activity, rising towards 3,000 or more for heavy physical work or cold-weather exposure, and falling to around 1,200 to 1,500 for a sedentary adult in a warm shelter. A useful planning figure for a sheltering household is 2,000 kilocalories per adult per day and 1,400 for a young child. For a family of four that is about 7,000 kilocalories daily, or roughly 100,000 kilocalories for a fourteen-day horizon. Rice at about 3,600 kilocalories per kilogram, pasta similar, and cooking oil at 8,800 make hitting that number by mass surprisingly easy: 30 kilograms of dry staples plus a few litres of oil supplies the bulk of a fortnight's energy for four people at a cost of perhaps 40 units of currency.

Calories alone, however, produce a miserable and eventually unhealthy plan. Protein needs run around 0.8 to 1 gram per kilogram of body weight per day; without it, a rice-and-oil diet leads to muscle wasting within weeks. Fat is essential and calorie-dense. Micronutrients matter over horizons beyond a few weeks: vitamin C deficiency produces clinical scurvy after roughly four to twelve weeks of near-total absence, which is a real historical hazard of long stored-food periods and is trivially prevented by a multivitamin, dried or tinned fruit, or sprouted legumes.

Shelf life dictates the tier. Below about six months, ordinary supermarket food works and should be managed as a deep pantry, buying what the household already eats and rotating it first-in first-out. Between six months and five years sit tinned goods, retort pouches, dried pasta, white rice, honey, sugar and salt. Above five years, and often to twenty-five or thirty when packed in sealed containers with oxygen absorbers in cool dry dark conditions, sit white rice, hard wheat, rolled oats, dried beans, powdered milk and freeze-dried products. Brown rice is a notable exception at roughly six months at room temperature, because its oil-bearing bran goes rancid.

Printed dates are widely misread. Best-before dates indicate quality, not safety, and most dry and tinned goods remain safe far beyond them, with gradual nutrient loss. Use-by dates on perishable products are safety limits and should be respected. Tins that are bulging, leaking, badly rusted or that hiss on opening should be discarded without tasting, because botulinum toxin is odourless and a fatal dose is measured in nanograms.

The practical rule is to build the horizon out of food the household eats routinely, extend it with cheap durable staples, and only then, if a longer tier is genuinely wanted, buy purpose-made long-life stock. Cooking capability must scale alongside: stored dry beans are worthless without fuel, water and a pot, and every stored-food plan needs a tested means of cooking without mains power.

sections.heading: Power, Heat, and the Seasonal Shape of the Horizon
sections.body:
Electricity is the service whose loss cascades furthest, because it silently underpins water pumping, heating controls, refrigeration, communications, payment systems and often sanitation. It is also the service where the required horizon depends most strongly on season and climate, since a summer outage is an inconvenience and a midwinter outage in a cold climate is a life-safety emergency within hours.

The critical distinction is between electricity as convenience and heat as survival. In a temperate winter, an unheated well-insulated dwelling typically drops from 20 degrees Celsius towards outdoor temperature over one to three days, and indoor temperatures below about 16 degrees begin to harm the elderly and the very young, with serious hypothermia risk emerging below about 12 degrees for vulnerable people over sustained periods. That timescale, not the length of the outage, sets the winter horizon. A household in Minnesota, Finland or the Scottish Highlands needs a heating answer measured in days; a household in Lisbon or Brisbane usually does not, and instead needs a cooling answer, since heat waves kill more people annually than cold in many regions and an indoor wet-bulb temperature above about 31 to 35 degrees is dangerous regardless of fitness.

Sizing electrical backup starts from load, not from a wish. Add up only what genuinely must run. A modern fridge-freezer uses roughly 1 to 1.5 kilowatt-hours per day; LED lighting for a household perhaps 0.3; phone and radio charging under 0.1; a gas boiler's pump and controls 0.5 to 1.5; a CPAP machine 0.2 to 0.5. A minimal survival load is therefore often 2 to 4 kilowatt-hours per day, which a 2-kilowatt-hour lithium power station plus 400 watts of solar can approximately sustain in decent light, while a 300-watt-hour power bank cannot. Whole-house comfort, including electric heating or air conditioning, runs 20 to 60 kilowatt-hours per day and requires a substantial generator and continuous fuel.

Fuel is the horizon constraint for generators, and it is severe. A 3-kilowatt inverter generator running an intermittent fridge-and-lights load burns roughly 4 to 8 litres of petrol per day. Fourteen days is therefore 60 to 110 litres, far beyond what most households can lawfully or safely store; typical domestic limits are of the order of 20 to 30 litres in approved containers, and untreated petrol degrades in three to six months. Propane stores indefinitely and is safer, diesel keeps a year or more with treatment, and this is why long-horizon power planning gravitates towards solar with battery storage, which has no consumable at all.

Heat without electricity deserves particular care. The safest household strategy is passive: reduce the heated volume to one room, seal it, insulate with duvets and blankets, use bodies and candles as low-grade heat sources, dress in layers with a hat, and sleep together. Any combustion heater must be either flued to outside or specifically certified for indoor use with an oxygen depletion sensor, and a battery carbon monoxide alarm is not optional in any household holding fuel-burning backup equipment.

sections.heading: Medication and Medical Supply: The Hardest Ceiling
sections.body:
For a substantial minority of households the medical horizon is the binding constraint, and unlike water or food it often cannot be extended by spending money, because the supply is controlled by prescribers, insurers and regulators rather than by shops.

The scale of the dependency is easy to underestimate. In most developed countries roughly half of adults take at least one prescription medicine regularly and around a quarter take three or more. For some of these, interruption is a minor inconvenience: a statin missed for a fortnight causes no acute harm. For others it is rapidly dangerous. Insulin-dependent diabetes progresses to ketoacidosis within roughly 12 to 48 hours without insulin. Abrupt withdrawal of anticonvulsants can precipitate status epilepticus. Stopping anticoagulants raises stroke risk within days. Abruptly ceasing beta blockers can cause rebound tachycardia and, in cardiac patients, infarction. Corticosteroid withdrawal after long-term use can precipitate an adrenal crisis. Missing antiretrovirals promotes resistance. Opioid and benzodiazepine withdrawal, while rarely fatal in the case of opioids, is medically serious for benzodiazepines and can be fatal.

The correct action is therefore to categorise your household's medicines into those where a gap is tolerable and those where it is not, in consultation with a prescriber, and to pursue extended supply only for the latter. Practical routes vary by jurisdiction but generally include requesting 90-day rather than 30-day dispensing, timing repeat requests as early as the system permits so that a rolling buffer accumulates, obtaining a documented emergency supply provision, and in some systems obtaining an explicit vacation or disaster override from an insurer. Many countries also permit pharmacists to dispense an emergency supply without a prescription in a declared emergency, and knowing whether yours does is worth checking in advance.

Storage conditions constrain the horizon further. Insulin requires refrigeration between 2 and 8 degrees Celsius for long-term storage, though most modern insulins tolerate room temperature up to about 25 to 30 degrees for 28 days once in use — a fact worth knowing precisely, because it converts a refrigeration emergency into a manageable 28-day window. Several biologic drugs, some vaccines and certain eye drops have similar cold-chain requirements. A cool box with frozen packs, or a 12-volt cooler on a battery, is a legitimate part of a medical horizon plan.

Beyond prescriptions, the medical kit should reflect duration. A short horizon needs trauma capability: pressure dressings, a tourniquet if trained, wound closure strips. A long horizon adds the mundane items that determine comfort and infection risk over weeks: oral rehydration salts, which are the single highest-value item in any long-duration kit because diarrhoeal illness is the classic emergency-shelter killer, simple analgesics, antihistamines, antiseptic, thermometer, and a good stock of whatever the household uses routinely. Stockpiling antibiotics for self-administration is widely marketed and generally a poor idea: wrong drug, wrong dose and wrong duration are the norm without diagnosis, and the resistance consequences are real.

sections.heading: Money, Documents, and the Administrative Horizon
sections.body:
The parts of a disruption that persist longest are usually administrative rather than physical, and households routinely prepare thoroughly for the first three days and not at all for the six months of paperwork that follow.

Cash is the immediate item. Electronic payment fails whenever power, telecommunications or bank systems fail, and it fails together across a whole area because the same infrastructure serves every shop. In events from the 2003 Northeast blackout to numerous hurricanes, cash was the only functioning medium for days. The planning quantity is the household's essential spending for the horizon, held in small denominations, because change is unavailable when tills are dark and a large note may be refused. For most households that is something between one and two weeks of groceries, fuel and incidentals — commonly 200 to 600 units of currency — stored securely at home, not in a bank, and reviewed so it does not slowly get spent.

Documents are the second item and are frequently the difference between a fast and a ruinous recovery. Insurance claims, government assistance, temporary accommodation, prescription re-issue, school enrolment and employment continuity all require identity and ownership evidence that may be destroyed along with the house. The core set is passports and identity cards, birth and marriage certificates, property deeds or tenancy agreements, insurance policies with policy numbers and the insurer's claim telephone number, vehicle registration, recent bank and utility statements, immunisation and key medical records, prescription lists with dosages, wills and powers of attorney, and photographs of every room and of serial numbers for a contents claim. These should exist in three forms: originals in a fire-resistant container, encrypted digital copies in cloud storage, and an encrypted copy on a USB drive in the grab bag.

Insurance itself deserves an annual check that most households never do. Standard household policies in most countries exclude flood, and in some regions exclude earthquake, requiring separate cover. Sum-insured figures drift out of date as building costs rise; underinsurance rates after major events are consistently reported above 50 per cent. Knowing your excess, your alternative-accommodation limit and your claim procedure before an event is worth more than most equipment purchases.

Finally, there is the income horizon, which for the median household is the likeliest severe disruption of all. The conventional financial-planning figure is three to six months of essential expenses held as accessible savings, and it is a preparedness measure in exactly the same sense as stored water. A household with three months of expenses saved and a fortnight of supplies is more resilient across the realistic range of misfortune than one with a year of freeze-dried food and no savings, because job loss, illness and family emergency are ordinary events while regional infrastructure collapse is not. The administrative horizon and the physical horizon should be set with the same seriousness, and where budget forces a choice, the evidence favours the financial one.

sections.heading: Rotation, Shelf Life, and the Maintenance Burden
sections.body:
The quiet killer of long horizons is maintenance. Every stored item has a decay clock, and the total maintenance burden scales roughly with the horizon while attention and enthusiasm do not. Plans fail not at the moment of the emergency but during the four uneventful years beforehand, when nobody checks anything.

The realistic burden for a well-run two-week household plan is perhaps two to four hours a year: rotating water, eating down and replacing food, testing torches and radios, replacing batteries, checking the first-aid kit, updating documents and reviewing the plan. A three-month plan roughly triples that. A one-year plan with fuel, a generator, bulk grain and water treatment equipment realistically demands one to two hours a month, indefinitely, and that estimate is the one most people fail to make before buying.

Specific decay clocks are worth knowing. Alkaline batteries last five to ten years in storage but leak potassium hydroxide when exhausted and will destroy the device they sit in, so equipment should be stored with batteries out; lithium primary cells last ten to twenty years and tolerate cold far better. Lithium-ion power banks and power stations self-discharge and degrade if stored fully charged or fully flat; store at roughly 50 to 60 per cent charge in a cool place and top up every six months. Lead-acid batteries sulphate and die if left discharged and need charging every three to six months. Petrol oxidises and gums carburettors in three to six months untreated, six to twelve with stabiliser; a generator should be run under load for twenty to thirty minutes quarterly and stored with fuel either stabilised or drained. Water in reused food-grade containers should be rotated every six to twelve months. Household bleach loses roughly 20 per cent of its available chlorine per year and is not reliable for disinfection after about a year, which makes it a poor long-horizon disinfectant compared with calcium hypochlorite granules or sodium dichloroisocyanurate tablets. Water filter elements have finite throughput and some have a shelf life once wetted. First-aid adhesives perish; sterile packs have expiry dates.

The design response is to minimise items with short clocks and to build the plan out of things you use anyway. A deep pantry rotates itself because it is the pantry. A power station that charges your laptop weekly stays healthy without a maintenance task. A camping stove used twice a summer is a tested camping stove. Conversely, sealed emergency ration bars, a generator never started, and drums of water in a crawl space are pure liabilities on the maintenance ledger.

A single annual review date, anchored to something memorable such as a clock change or a birthday, catches most of it. Write the list of decay clocks once, put dates on the containers with a marker, and accept that a horizon you will actually maintain at fourteen days is worth more than one you will neglect at three hundred and sixty-five.

sections.heading: Household Constraints and the Horizon You Can Actually Sustain
sections.body:
A horizon is only real if the specific household, in its specific dwelling, with its specific budget and abilities, can hold it. General advice systematically assumes a house with a garage, a car, a garden and a middle income, and most households do not have all four.

Storage volume is the first hard limit. Fourteen days of water for a family of four is about a quarter of a cubic metre and a fifth of a tonne; a one-bedroom flat may have nowhere to put it, and an upper floor may have loading limits worth respecting. The realistic responses are to reduce the stored-water horizon and add treatment capability, to use the dwelling's own hidden storage such as the water heater tank, to distribute supplies under beds and in wardrobes in small containers rather than seeking one big space, and to accept that an apartment household's water horizon may be three days stored plus a filter rather than fourteen days stored.

Budget is the second. Preparedness marketing implies large purchases, but the highest-value items are cheap: a battery or wind-up radio, a torch with lithium cells, a water filter, oral rehydration salts, a carbon monoxide alarm, a first-aid kit, cash, and a deep pantry of food already eaten. A household on a tight budget should buy in that order and can reach a genuinely competent fourteen-day position for a modest sum accumulated over months. Buying a few extra tins each shopping trip builds a pantry invisibly.

Physical and cognitive constraints reshape the plan rather than reducing it. A person who cannot carry 20 litres of water needs smaller containers and more of them, or a source on the same floor. A powered wheelchair, stairlift, oxygen concentrator, dialysis schedule or CPAP machine converts electricity from convenience to life support and should trigger both a battery plan and registration on the utility's priority services register, which most utilities operate and most eligible customers never join. A household member with dementia may need the plan to be executed entirely by someone else, which means writing it down for that person.

Household composition sets consumption. Infants need formula, which cannot be improvised safely, and sterilising capability; a fortnight's formula is a specific, non-substitutable stock. Pets need their own water and food, roughly 50 millilitres of water per kilogram of body weight per day for a dog, and a carrier for evacuation; shelters that refuse pets are a documented cause of people refusing to evacuate, which is why many jurisdictions changed the law after Hurricane Katrina.

Tenure matters too. Renters cannot install a wood stove, a rainwater tank or a fixed generator, and should concentrate on portable, transferable capability. Whatever the constraints, the honest move is to write the achievable horizon down as it actually is, with the shortfalls named, rather than to adopt a standard number that the household has no means of meeting. A documented three-day plan that works beats an imagined thirty-day plan that does not.

sections.heading: Failure Modes: Horizon Creep, Sunk Costs, and Being Wrong
sections.body:
Preparedness planning has characteristic ways of going wrong, and most of them are failures of judgement rather than of equipment.

Horizon creep is the most common. A household sets fourteen days, reaches it, feels the satisfaction of competence, and reaches for thirty, then ninety, then a year, without ever revisiting whether the local hazard profile justifies any of it. The extra effort displaces higher-value work — insurance review, savings, fitness, first-aid training, knowing the neighbours — and the maintenance burden eventually exceeds the household's willingness, at which point the whole plan decays together. The corrective is the written horizon with its stated justification. If the number changes, the justification must change first.

Sunk-cost attachment is the second. Money spent on a generator, a bunker, a stock of a particular food, or a specific water system creates an incentive to build the plan around the purchase rather than around the risk. The clearest symptom is a plan that has an elaborate answer for one hazard and no answer at all for the likeliest one. Periodically re-deriving the plan from the hazard list, ignoring what has already been bought, exposes this.

Skill and capital are routinely confused. Equipment is easy to buy and hard to use. A water filter nobody has assembled, a generator nobody has started, a radio nobody has tuned, and a fire extinguisher nobody has discharged are all approximately worthless. The single highest-return preparedness activity for most households is not a purchase but a rehearsal: run a weekend on stored supplies with the mains breaker off, and discover that the tin opener is electric, that the torch batteries are dead, that nobody knows where the stopcock is, and that the plan assumed a car that was out of fuel. Every such discovery is cheap now and expensive later.

Individualism is the third failure. The strongest empirical predictor of household outcomes in disasters is not stockpile depth but social connection. Research following the 1995 Chicago heat wave, in which around 700 people died, found that neighbourhoods with similar poverty and demographics diverged sharply in death rates according to social cohesion and the presence of places where people encountered one another. In practice neighbours restore power, share generators, check on the elderly, lend tools and provide information long before any agency arrives. A plan that treats the household as an island is worse than one that includes three named neighbours and a rough agreement about who checks on whom.

Finally, accept that the horizon will sometimes be wrong. The event will be longer, or a different shape, or will arrive while you are away from home. The defence is not a bigger number but flexibility: general-purpose capability, a written plan the whole household knows, a habit of updating from real events rather than from marketing, and the willingness to say plainly that a given scenario exceeds what this household can cover alone, and that the answer to it is evacuation or assistance rather than stores.

guides.safetyNote: Water treatment, fuel storage, generator use and medication stockpiling all carry real hazards. Never run a generator, charcoal grill or unvented fuel heater indoors or in an attached garage — carbon monoxide from a single portable generator can reach lethal concentrations in an enclosed space within minutes. Store petrol only in approved containers outside living space. Do not stockpile prescription medication by skipping doses or by taking expired antibiotics on your own judgement; discuss extended supply with a prescriber and a pharmacist. Follow national guidance on drinking-water disinfection doses precisely, and never mix bleach with other cleaning chemicals.

guides.title: Mapping Hazards Around Your Home Address
guides.summary: How to build a personal hazard map of everything that can hurt you within reach of your own address — floods, fire, earth, weather, industry, and infrastructure — and turn it into routes, triggers, and decisions.

sections.heading: Why Your Address Has Its Own Disaster Profile
sections.body: Disasters are usually described at the scale of regions: a hurricane strikes a coastline, an earthquake shakes a metropolitan area, a wildfire burns a county. But nobody experiences a disaster at that scale. You experience it at an address, and two houses a few hundred metres apart can have radically different fates in the same event. One sits two metres above the floodplain and stays dry while its neighbour takes water to the windowsills. One backs onto a brush-choked slope and receives the ember storm; another, across a six-lane road, does not. One lies inside the toxic plume footprint of a rail line that carries chlorine tank cars at 3 a.m.; the house a kilometre crosswind was never in danger. Risk science expresses this with a simple product: risk equals hazard times exposure times vulnerability. The hazard, a flood or spill or quake, is set by geography and chance and is largely beyond your influence. Exposure, whether the hazard can physically reach you, your family, and the things you depend on, is a property of your specific location, and it is knowable in advance with ordinary effort. Vulnerability, how badly the contact would hurt you, is the part preparation can change. Mapping hazards around your home is the systematic act of learning your exposure, and it is the single highest-leverage step in household preparedness because every other decision depends on it: what supplies to hold, which insurance riders matter, which direction you would drive, what an odd smell at night should make you do. Emergency managers do exactly this exercise for whole jurisdictions; every county or municipal hazard mitigation plan begins with a hazard identification and risk assessment, and those documents are public. What almost nobody does is repeat the exercise at household scale, where it is both easier and more actionable. The payoff is not paranoia but calibration. Most people carry a hazard model assembled from news imagery, which over-weights dramatic distant events and under-weights the mundane local ones that actually dominate the statistics: the creek that floods every decade, the propane dealer at the edge of town, the dead pines leaning toward the power line. Studies of disaster response repeatedly find that households which had thought concretely about their specific situation act faster and make better choices under stress, largely because they are not solving the problem for the first time while frightened. A hazard map also compounds: once drawn, it turns every news story, weather alert, and siren into a query you can answer in seconds, because you already know whether the thing being warned about can reach your ground. This guide walks through the full sweep, natural hazards in water, fire, earth, and sky, then the human-made ones in industry, transport, and infrastructure, then how to find authoritative data, survey the ground in person, draw the map itself, and convert it into routes, thresholds, and habits that hold up when the day comes.

sections.heading: Thinking in Rings: The Four Scales That Matter
sections.body: A useful hazard map is organised by distance, because distance is what determines both what can reach you and how much warning you will get. Four nested rings cover nearly everything, and each ring has its own characteristic hazards, information sources, and decisions. The innermost ring is roughly 50 metres: your own structure and lot. Here live the hazards you can touch: the water heater that needs strapping in earthquake country, the tree limb over the bedroom, the dryer vent packed with lint, the slope behind the retaining wall, the gas meter and its shutoff, the storm drain at the kerb that backs up in cloudbursts. Ring-one hazards rarely make the news, yet ordinary house fires, falls, and carbon monoxide kill far more people year by year than every spectacular hazard combined, and this is also the only ring where you hold direct authority to fix things. The second ring is about 500 metres: your immediate neighbourhood, the distance you can walk in five minutes carrying a child. Here the questions become relational: what is uphill, upwind, and upstream of you? A creek, a fuel station, an auto-body shop with solvent drums, a neighbour's dying eucalyptus, a slope of unmaintained brush. This is the ring that determines whether somebody else's bad night becomes yours, and walking it on foot reveals what no database lists. The third ring is about 5 kilometres: your community. This ring holds the rail corridor, the highway with hazardous cargo, the industrial park, the tank farm, the dam or levee, the airport approach path, the hospital and fire stations you would depend on, and the chokepoints, bridges, underpasses, single access roads, that control whether you can leave. Most plume, blast, and fast-flood scenarios play out inside ring three, and most of the official data described in this guide addresses it. The outermost ring is about 50 kilometres: your region. Here sit the big upstream dam, the nuclear plant with its ten-mile and fifty-mile planning zones, the wildland fire complex that can travel astonishing distances in a wind event, the volcano, and the regional infrastructure, transmission corridors, water supplies, refineries, whose failure reaches you as outage rather than impact. Ring four rarely demands that you flee; it demands that you can endure disruption and receive warnings. The rings also sort hazards by geometry. Point sources, a plant, a tank, a well pad, project risk outward in circles or wind-driven plumes. Corridors, rivers, rail lines, highways, pipelines, fault traces, project it in ribbons; living 200 metres from a rail line matters far more than living 2 kilometres from a rail yard. Area hazards, seismic shaking, hail, heat, pandemic, cover everything at once and are mapped by intensity rather than boundary. As you research, tag every hazard you find with its ring and its geometry; that pair of labels does most of the analytic work.

sections.heading: Water: Reading Flood Risk at Your Doorstep
sections.body: Flooding is the most common and most expensive disaster on Earth, and it comes in flavours with very different signatures at a given address. Riverine flooding is the slow kind: a river rises over days as its watershed drains, and the danger zone is the floodplain, the flat land the river built with its own sediment and periodically reclaims. Flash flooding is the fast kind, driven by intense rainfall over small, steep, or paved catchments; a dry wash, an urban culvert, or a canyon can go from damp to lethal in under an hour, sometimes from a storm you never saw because it fell upstream. Coastal flooding arrives as storm surge, wind-driven ocean water that behaves like a temporary tide of one to nine metres depending on storm and bathymetry. Urban or pluvial flooding is rain falling faster than drains can swallow, and it happens on hills as readily as in valleys; basements and underpasses are its signature victims. Groundwater flooding seeps up through soil weeks after wet seasons. Official flood maps address mainly the riverine and coastal kinds. In the United States, FEMA's Flood Insurance Rate Maps classify land by annual exceedance probability; the so-called 100-year zone means a 1 percent chance of flooding in any given year, which compounds to roughly a 26 percent chance over a 30-year mortgage, odds nobody would accept at poker. Other countries publish equivalents, such as the Environment Agency's flood map for England or state flood portals elsewhere; find yours by searching the national mapping agency plus the word flood. Read such maps with respect and suspicion at once: they encode serious hydrology, but many are decades old, assume past rainfall statistics in a changing climate, ignore pluvial flooding entirely, and stop at the edge of small streams that were never studied. Around one in three US flood-damage claims arises outside any mapped high-risk zone. So supplement the map with the terrain itself. Elevation above the nearest water, not distance from it, is what protects you; free topographic viewers let you read your lot's elevation and trace where water flowing downhill from your roof would go. Walk your neighbourhood in heavy rain once, deliberately: watch which gutters overtop, which yards pond, where the creek runs brown and loud. Look for the archaeology of past water: stained foundations, high-water marks on bridge piers, replaced lower drywall in older buildings, and ask long-term neighbours the year the water last came and how high. Note the infrastructure your dryness depends on, the culvert under the road, the pump station, the levee, and learn who maintains it and what happens when it clogs or fails, because a blocked culvert converts a nuisance storm into a neighbourhood dam-break. Finally, mark on your map the depth that matters: fifteen centimetres of moving water can knock an adult off their feet, sixty can float a car, and most flood deaths are vehicles driven into water whose depth the driver misjudged at night.

sections.heading: Fire: The Wildland Interface and the Ember Problem
sections.body: Wildfire risk at an address is often misunderstood as a question of whether the flame front can reach you. In the fires that destroy whole neighbourhoods, most homes are not touched by the front at all; they are ignited by embers, burning fragments lofted by the fire's convection column and carried on the wind, in extreme events more than a kilometre or two ahead of the flames. Post-fire investigations, including detailed studies after California's 2017 and 2018 fire sieges, repeatedly attribute the majority of home losses to ember ignition of the home itself or of something within a few metres of it: leaf-filled gutters, juniper foundation plantings, wooden fences that lead flame to the wall like a fuse, firewood stacked against siding, and vents that inhale sparks into attics. Your fire mapping therefore starts at the house and works outward through what researchers call the home ignition zone. Ring zero to 1.5 metres should hold nothing combustible, no mulch, no shrubs, no stored anything, with ember-resistant vent mesh of about 3 millimetres and no gaps in eaves or shingles. From 1.5 to 9 metres, vegetation should be lean, green, watered, and discontinuous, with tree limbs pruned well off the ground so surface fire cannot climb into crowns. From 9 to 30 metres, the goal is broken fuel continuity: spaced trees, mown grass, no ladder of brush connecting ground to canopy. Beyond your lot, map the wildland-urban interface geometry around you: how close does continuous natural fuel, forest, chaparral, grassland, even an overgrown vacant block, come to your ring one and two, and from which compass direction.
