Fire moves with wind and uphill; on steep ground its spread rate roughly doubles for every 10 degrees of slope, because rising heat pre-dries the fuel above. A house at the top of a brushy slope, in the path of the region's hot dry seasonal wind, holds close to the worst hand possible. Learn your region's fire weather pattern by name, the Santa Ana, the Diablo, the mistral, the foehn, the Australian northerly, because the disaster days are wind days, and red flag warnings are your map's activation signal. Check official wildfire hazard severity maps where they exist, many jurisdictions publish them at parcel resolution, but also read history: previous fire perimeters are mapped and fires rerun the same terrain. Mark your evacuation geometry with special care, since fire evacuations fail at chokepoints; a hillside suburb with one winding exit road can trap hundreds of cars, as happened catastrophically in Paradise, California in 2018, when 85 people died. Identify two exits in different compass directions if they exist, and a last-resort refuge, a large car park, a sports field, a body of water, for the scenario where the road itself is cut. Ember-proofing the structure and knowing the wind are worth more than any amount of hose.

sections.heading: Earth: Quakes, Slides, Sinkholes, and the Ground Itself
sections.body: Hazards from the ground are the least visible on a casual walk, which makes the research step matter most. Earthquake exposure begins with regional maps, national seismic hazard models published by geological surveys, which express risk as the shaking intensity with a given probability over decades. But the regional number is only half the story, because local geology amplifies or muffles shaking. Soft sediments, old lake beds, artificial fill, and river deposits can amplify ground motion several-fold relative to bedrock a street away; Mexico City in 1985 was devastated by a quake 350 kilometres distant largely because its lakebed clays rang like a bowl of jelly. Water-saturated sandy soils add liquefaction, in which shaking makes the ground temporarily behave as a fluid: buildings settle and tilt, buried tanks float upward, and roads split. Many urban areas publish liquefaction and amplification susceptibility maps; find whether your lot sits on rock, stiff soil, or fill, and note that unreinforced masonry, houses not bolted to their foundations, and heavy tile roofs are the classic structural victims. Inside ring one, earthquake mapping means an inventory: the water heater that needs strapping, the tall furniture unanchored beside beds, the masonry chimney, the gas line whose shutoff you have never located, and the crawl-space cripple walls that retrofit crews bolt and brace. Landslides obey simpler rules: they need slope, water, and weak or disturbed material. Natural slopes steeper than about 15 to 20 degrees deserve attention anywhere; cut slopes above roads, slopes logged or burned in the past few years, and any hillside with tilted trees, cracked ground, bulging toes, or doors that stick after wet weeks are telling you they move. Debris flows, fast slurries of mud and boulders, follow drainages below burned or saturated slopes and can travel kilometres; if you live on an alluvial fan at a canyon mouth in fire country, the burn scar upstream is your hazard for several wet seasons after the smoke clears. Karst terrain, limestone dissolved by groundwater, produces sinkholes, common in Florida, parts of the UK Midlands, and much of the world's carbonate geology; local geological surveys map karst, and sudden circular ponds, leaning fence lines, and cracked slabs are field signs. Expansive clay soils, which swell wet and shrink dry, quietly cause more structural damage in many regions than earthquakes do, cracking foundations through seasonal cycles. Finally, include the ground's invisible export: radon, a radioactive gas seeping from certain rock types into basements, is the second-leading cause of lung cancer in several countries; geological surveys publish radon potential maps, and a measurement costs little. None of these hazards announces itself on the day you buy or rent; all of them are discoverable in an afternoon of map work plus one observant walk.

sections.heading: Sky: Wind, Hail, Ice, Heat, and Lightning
sections.body: Weather hazards are area hazards, they arrive over your whole district at once, so mapping them is less about drawing boundaries and more about knowing your local climatology and your address's particular aggravating factors. Start with wind. Learn which severe wind mechanisms your region actually produces: tropical cyclones on warm coasts, tornadoes in the interior of continents with the necessary clash of air masses, derechos, long-lived straight-line windstorms that can flatten trees along a 400-kilometre swath, and downslope windstorms in the lee of mountain ranges. Historical tornado tracks and hurricane strike frequencies are mapped and public; what turns the regional statistic into an address-level fact is your exposure inventory: the mature trees within falling distance of the roof and driveway, the neighbour's trampoline, the age and attachment of your own roof covering, and whether anything on your lot becomes a missile at 120 kilometres per hour. Mark the interior refuge too, the smallest lowest windowless room, and note that in mobile or lightweight homes the plan must be to leave for sturdier shelter, since they account for a grossly disproportionate share of wind fatalities. Hail follows recognisable geographic alleys, insurance and meteorological services map claim frequency, and matters for roofs, skylights, gardens, and any vehicle without covered parking. Ice storms are among the most underrated mapped hazards: freezing rain loads every branch and cable with centimetres of ice, and the difference between inconvenience and a two-week regional blackout is written in the trees around your local distribution lines; if your power arrives overhead through a corridor of mature, brittle trees, your outage risk is structural, not statistical. Snow load matters at the address level through roof pitch and structure age, and through the question of whether your street is a ploughing priority or an afterthought. Heat is the quiet outlier: in many developed countries heat waves kill more people than all other weather combined, and exposure varies block by block through the urban heat island effect, dense pavement and scarce canopy can run a neighbourhood 5 to 7 degrees Celsius hotter than a leafy district across town. Map your dwelling's thermal reality honestly: top-floor flats, west-facing glass, dark roofs, and homes without cooling put elderly occupants at genuine risk, and the practical annotations are the coolest room, the shaded side, and the nearest public cooled space. Lightning deserves one line on the map and one habit: note the tall isolated objects near your outdoor spaces, and adopt the 30-30 rule, if thunder follows flash within 30 seconds, be indoors, and stay there 30 minutes after the last thunder. For every sky hazard, the warning system is the map's activation layer: know the difference between a watch, conditions are favourable, and a warning, the event is occurring or imminent, and decide in advance what each one triggers at your address.

sections.heading: Industrial Neighbours: Fixed Facilities and What They Store
sections.body: Every developed area contains buildings whose contents, released suddenly, would redraw the map around them, and most people cannot name the ones within five kilometres of their bed. The heavy hitters are well-known categories: refineries and fuel tank farms; chemical manufacturers and distributors; water and wastewater treatment plants, which historically stored chlorine gas by the ton, though many have converted to safer bleach processes; cold-storage warehouses and food processors running ammonia refrigeration; propane and LPG dealers; fertiliser depots holding ammonium nitrate, the chemical behind the 2013 West, Texas explosion that levelled homes over a wide radius and the 2020 Beirut port blast; grain elevators, whose dust can explode with the force of a bomb; and electroplating, pool-supply, and agricultural-chemical operations that look like ordinary sheds. The scenarios worth mapping fall into three physical types, each with its own footprint geometry. Toxic release produces a downwind plume, ammonia, chlorine, hydrogen sulfide, or smoke from a chemical warehouse fire, whose shape is set by wind and stability; a plume can be dangerous at kilometres downwind while a house a few hundred metres crosswind is untouched. Fire and thermal radiation threaten mainly within hundreds of metres. Blast, from vapour clouds, compressed gases, or energetic solids, breaks windows and injures with glass at distances the fire itself never reaches. Fortunately, industrial hazards are the best-documented category on your whole map. Many jurisdictions operate community right-to-know regimes: in the United States, EPCRA requires facilities holding threshold quantities of hazardous substances to file annual Tier II inventories with local emergency planning committees, the EPA's Toxics Release Inventory is searchable online by address, and high-hazard facilities file Risk Management Plans whose worst-case release radii are public in reading rooms. The European Union's Seveso directives require comparable disclosure and community information; other countries vary, but fire services everywhere maintain pre-plans you can often learn about simply by asking. Your local emergency management agency's hazard mitigation plan will usually name the facilities it worries about, and a methodical hour with satellite imagery, look for tank farms, rail spurs into plants, rows of cylinders, plus street-view reading of signage will find the rest. For each facility within roughly five kilometres, record on your map: what it likely holds, which direction it lies from you, and, crucially, your prevailing winds, because a plant ten kilometres upwind on the dominant wind can matter more than one two kilometres downwind. Then attach the single most important response fact: for a toxic plume, the default life-saving action is usually shelter-in-place, indoors, doors and windows shut, ventilation off, in an interior room, because driving through a plume to evacuate multiplies your dose. Sirens, reverse-911 calls, or an unexplained chemical odour with an upwind facility on your map should trigger that response without deliberation.

sections.heading: Corridors: Rail, Road, Pipelines, and Flight Paths
sections.body: Hazardous materials do not only sit in facilities; they move, and the corridors they move along project a ribbon of risk through neighbourhoods that contain no industry at all. Rail is the corridor most worth respecting. A single freight train can carry a hundred tank cars, and any given train may include chlorine, anhydrous ammonia, LPG, crude oil, or molten sulphur; derailments are routine events measured in the hundreds per year in large rail networks, and while most are harmless, the exceptional ones, Lac-Mégantic in 2013, where a runaway crude train destroyed a town centre and killed 47, East Palestine in 2023, define the stakes. If a rail line passes within about 1.5 kilometres of your address, mark it, note which way is downwind of it in your prevailing winds, and treat any night-time boom, hiss, or chemical smell from that direction as a signal to shelter or move crosswind, not to walk toward the interesting glow. Highways designated as hazmat routes carry tankers of fuel and chemicals; the address-level facts that matter are proximity to interchanges and steep grades, where crashes cluster, and whether your street would become the detour when the highway closes. Pipelines are the invisible corridor: transmission lines for natural gas, refined products, and crude cross astonishing amounts of ordinary suburbia, marked only by small posts at road crossings bearing the operator's name and an emergency number. National mapping systems, in the US the National Pipeline Mapping System, show transmission lines near an address; distribution gas mains under your own street are smaller but nearer, and the practical knowledge is the smell of mercaptan odourant, the rule to leave immediately without operating switches, and the location of your own meter valve. San Bruno, California, 2010, a corroded transmission main under a residential street, eight dead, demonstrated that this corridor deserves a line on the map even where nothing is visible. Flight paths matter mainly within a few kilometres of runway ends, where approach and departure tracks concentrate; the risk is small but the geometry is knowable, and airports also matter on your map as noise, as traffic generators, and as the occasional source of fuel-dumping and cargo incidents. For every corridor, the mapping act is the same: draw the line, shade a band around it, 300 metres for immediate blast and fire effects, 1.5 kilometres for toxic plume potential on rail and major pipelines, note your bearing and prevailing wind relative to it, and identify which of your routine locations, home, school, workplace, commute, sit inside the band. Corridors also cut: the same rail line and highway are barriers that a closure or a derailment can turn into walls between you and your family, so mark the crossing points and the alternates that avoid them.

sections.heading: Infrastructure You Depend On: Dams, Grids, and Water
sections.body: Some of the most consequential features on your hazard map never touch your address directly; they fail at a distance and reach you as water, darkness, or silence in the taps. Dams lead the category. If any significant dam sits upstream of you, and river valleys mean that many addresses have one, its failure inundation zone may include your neighbourhood, and those zones are formally mapped: dam owners of high-hazard structures are generally required to maintain emergency action plans with inundation maps, and many are public or obtainable through your emergency management office. The 2017 Oroville spillway crisis in California put 188,000 people under evacuation orders in hours; people who already knew they lived in the inundation zone left early and calmly. Levees deserve the same respect inverted: land behind a levee is dry precisely because a wall is holding, floods there are rarer but deeper and faster when they come, and levee districts publish their ratings. The electric grid is the dependency that turns every other hazard worse. Map your own dependency first: what in your household actually fails without power, heat, well pump, refrigerated medicine, medical devices, garage door, and then map the local fragility: overhead lines through tree corridors fail in ice and wind; a single substation feeding an isolated area is a single point of failure; regions with wildfire-driven public safety power shutoffs publish their likely zones. Water systems fail in two directions: supply, pumps need power, mains break in freezes and quakes, and contamination, boil-water notices follow floods with regularity. Know where your water comes from, a municipal main, a private well with an electric pump, and what your household would drink for three days if it stopped. Wastewater backs up when lift stations lose power; a simple backflow valve is a map-driven purchase for low-lying homes on gravity sewers. Communications fail with power but on a lag, cell towers carry batteries for hours, not days, so the map should note where coverage from a different carrier or a working landline exists, and households that care add a battery AM/FM radio as the layer of last resort. Two special cases earn explicit rings. If you live within roughly 16 kilometres of a nuclear power plant, you are inside a formally planned emergency zone with published evacuation routes, siren systems, and potassium iodide distribution, and within about 80 kilometres you are in the ingestion-planning zone, where the concern is contaminated food and water rather than direct exposure; both zones and their instructions are public documents worth reading once. And everywhere, the municipal services you would call on, fire stations, hospitals with emergency departments, police, matter as travel times: mark the nearest two of each and notice what lies between you and them, because the bridge that floods or the rail crossing that blocks is also the barrier between your emergency and its response.

sections.heading: Finding the Data: Records, Maps, and Institutional Memory
sections.body: Nearly everything this guide asks you to learn is already written down; the craft is knowing which drawer to open. Start with your local government's hazard mitigation plan, required in the US by the Disaster Mitigation Act of 2000 and paralleled by civil-protection risk assessments elsewhere. It is a public document, usually posted on the county or municipal website, and its hazard identification chapters have already done your regional homework: which floods, fires, quakes, storms, and facilities the professionals worry about, with maps. Read it once and your ring three and four are half done. National portals fill in parcel-level detail: flood map services, seismic hazard and liquefaction viewers, wildfire hazard severity layers, landslide inventories, radon potential, pipeline mapping systems, and toxic facility registries, each searchable by address in most developed countries. Insurance is a second, cynical but efficient lens: ask an agent what drives premiums at your address; actuaries have already priced your hazards, and a flood or earthquake rider's cost is information. Historical memory beats models for local specifics. Local newspaper archives, many digitised and searchable, record every flood, tornado track, plant fire, and evacuation of the past century; search your street and district names with words like flood, fire, evacuate, and derail. Libraries and historical societies hold photographs of past high water with visible landmarks. And the deepest archive is human: neighbours of thirty years, volunteer firefighters, and public works crews know where the water goes, which slope moves, and which intersection floods first, and they enjoy being asked. Institutional sources for specific hazards are worth naming. Fire services will often tell you your response time and hydrant situation. Utility outage maps watched across a season reveal which circuits fail chronically. Dam emergency action plans live with emergency management offices. School and workplace emergency plans tell you where your family members will be taken if you cannot reach them. As you gather, keep a source log, where each fact came from and its date, because data ages at different rates: geology is effectively permanent, flood maps drift over decades, facility inventories change annually, and construction changes drainage overnight. Treat conflicting sources as a finding in itself; when the flood map says dry and the neighbour says wet, the neighbour usually wins, and the discrepancy is exactly where your personal map adds value. An evening of this work per ring produces a picture of your surroundings that very few households, and honestly not every local official, actually possesses.
ingredients: Local hazard mitigation plan or civil-protection risk assessment (county/municipal website)
National flood map portal for your country, plus a topographic/elevation viewer
Seismic hazard, liquefaction, landslide, and radon potential maps (geological survey website)
Wildfire hazard severity map and historical fire perimeter viewer, where applicable
Toxic/hazardous facility registries and community right-to-know filings (e.g., TRI, Tier II, Seveso)
National pipeline mapping system and rail-line maps
Dam inundation and levee information from your emergency management office
Utility outage maps and public safety power shutoff zone maps
Local newspaper archive access (library card often suffices) and long-term neighbours' recollections
A source log: notebook or spreadsheet recording each fact, its source, and its date

sections.heading: Walking the Ground: The Field Survey Maps Cannot Replace
sections.body: Databases see categories; only feet see particulars. After the desk research, walk your first two rings deliberately, ideally twice, once in fine weather and once in foul, because rain, wind, and darkness are the map's operating conditions. Go slowly and look at water's infrastructure first: every storm drain, culvert, ditch, and creek crossing within 500 metres. Note which drain grates are already half-blocked with leaves, where the culvert under the road is small relative to the ditch feeding it, where previous water has left silt lines, wrack, bent grass, or gravel fans across pavement. Look uphill from your lot and ask the oldest question in hydrology: where does water want to go, and am I standing in its way? Then read fuels and fire paths: continuous brush or dry grass running from open land toward structures, wooden fences connecting vegetation to houses, gutters visibly full of litter, trees overhanging roofs and power lines. Utility hardware deserves a hard look: leaning poles, trees grown through lines, transformers on poles above parked cars, and the pipeline marker posts at road crossings that almost nobody consciously sees; read the operator names and emergency numbers on them. Industrial and commercial buildings reveal themselves by signage and hardware: hazard diamonds (the NFPA 704 placard's blue, red, and yellow numbers rank health, flammability, and reactivity from 0 to 4), rows of gas cylinders, refrigeration plants humming behind food businesses, tanker deliveries at odd hours. At rail crossings, read the blue emergency notification sign, it carries the railway's emergency number and the crossing's unique identifier, and notice what actually rides the line for a few minutes: intermodal boxes are one risk profile, black tank cars are another. Survey your exit geometry as a driver and again as a pedestrian: where are the pinch points, the single bridge, the underpass that floods, the intersection that gridlocks at school pickup, and what is the on-foot route out if roads are blocked or gridlocked? Time the walk to your two nearest fire stations and your designated family rally points. Note the human landscape as frankly as the physical one: the neighbour with a generator and chainsaw, the retired nurse two doors down, the household that will need help evacuating, because in every studied disaster the first responders are neighbours, and knowing who is where is preparedness of the most literal kind. Photograph what you find, phones geotag automatically, and annotate the map the same evening while memory is fresh. Repeat a compressed version of the walk each season; vegetation, construction, and drainage change, and a survey has a shelf life of about a year. The walk routinely produces the map's most valuable single entries, and they are almost never things any database contained.

sections.heading: Building the Map Itself: A Working Procedure
sections.body: The physical artefact matters. A hazard picture that lives scattered across browser bookmarks and good intentions is not usable at 2 a.m. in a power cut; a single annotated map, on paper, with a digital twin, is. The base can be humble: printed street maps at two scales, or screenshots from a free map service. Draw your rings lightly, then build the map in layers, using a consistent colour code, blue for water, red for fire, brown for earth, purple for industrial and corridor hazards, so the finished sheet reads at a glance. Annotate sparsely: a symbol and two or three words, chlorine, upwind winter, or culvert chokes here, beat a paragraph. The map earns its keep through the response layer: exits in at least two compass directions with their pinch points marked, rally points, utility shutoffs, and the pre-decided actions written on the margin as if-then sentences. Keep the paper copy where the household can find it in the dark, tape a duplicate inside a cupboard door, and keep the digital twin on phones and one cloud location. Build it once properly in a weekend; maintain it in minutes per season thereafter.
steps: Obtain base maps at two scales: one detailed sheet covering your lot and 500-metre ring, one regional sheet covering 5 to 50 kilometres. Print them; paper is the operating format.
Mark your address and draw the four rings (50 m, 500 m, 5 km, 50 km) lightly. Add a north arrow and, critically, your prevailing wind directions by season, since plumes and fire run downwind.

Layer water hazards in blue: flood zones from the official map, your own elevation, drainage paths, culverts and drains found on your walk, and historical high-water marks from archives and neighbours.

Layer fire in red where applicable: the wildland interface edge, continuous fuels, the direction of the dangerous seasonal wind, previous fire perimeters, and your two evacuation exits with pinch points circled.

Layer earth in brown: soil or fill amplification and liquefaction zones, steep or moving slopes, karst, and a house-level inventory list (water heater strap, unanchored furniture, gas shutoff location) written in the margin.

Layer industry and corridors in purple: each significant facility with its likely contents and bearing from you; rail lines, hazmat highways, and pipelines with a shaded band; dam inundation zones from the emergency action plan.

Add the response layer in black: two exit routes in different directions, family rally points near and far, shutoff locations for gas, water, and power, nearest fire stations and emergency departments, and the shelter-in-place room.
Write the trigger table on the margin: five to ten if-then lines pairing each mapped hazard with its pre-decided action and the warning source that activates it.
Duplicate: photograph every sheet, laminate a vehicle copy, post one inside a cupboard door, and file the source log with dates.
Walk one household member who did not build the map through it until they can use it unaided; a map only one person can read is a single point of failure.

sections.heading: From Map to Decisions: Thresholds, Triggers, and Routes
sections.body: A map describes; a plan decides. The bridge between them is the trigger: a pre-committed pairing of an observable condition with an action, written down while calm, so that the decision under stress is recognition rather than reasoning. Psychologically this matters more than any equipment purchase, because the documented failure mode of humans in emergencies is not panic but delay, normalcy bias, the strong tendency to interpret ambiguous signals as fine and to wait for one more confirmation; survivors of disasters from hotel fires to tsunamis are disproportionately the people who moved first. Good triggers are specific, observable, and binary. Vague: if flooding gets bad, we might leave. Usable: if the river gauge at the Mill Street bridge reads 4.2 metres and rising, or if water covers the crown of our street, we leave for the far rally point via the northern route, now. Build one trigger line per mapped hazard. For the industrial plume: sirens, an official alert, or a strong chemical odour with the wind from the plant's bearing means indoors, windows shut, HVAC off, interior room, radio on, and we do not drive. For wildfire: a red flag warning pre-stages the vehicle fuelled and facing out with the go-bags loaded; an evacuation warning for our zone means we leave then, not at the mandatory order, because the mandatory stage is when the roads jam. For the earthquake region: any shaking strong enough to make standing hard is itself the trigger, drop, cover, hold on, then gas check, then the street-side rally point; near a coast, strong shaking longer than about 20 seconds is a tsunami trigger and high ground is the action without waiting for sirens. Routes deserve the same pre-commitment. For each likely direction of threat, know your primary and alternate exits and, harder, the direction you would not go, toward the rail line, through the underpass that floods, into the canyon road with one lane. Agree rally points at two distances, one near the home for fires and one outside the district for area evacuations, plus an out-of-region phone contact everyone reports to, because long-distance calls and texts often work when local networks are saturated. Assign the household's division of labour in advance, who carries the documents, who handles pets, who checks on the neighbour who cannot drive, and cap the loading of the car with a hard time limit written on the trigger table. None of this requires drama; a family that has walked its two routes once and can recite five if-then lines has converted its map into perhaps fifteen minutes of earned lead time, and lead time is the commodity that decides outcomes.

sections.heading: Keeping the Map Alive: Review Cycles and Change Detection
sections.body: A hazard map is a snapshot of a moving scene, and its failure mode is quiet obsolescence: the map stays crisp on the cupboard door while the world it describes drifts away from it. Build maintenance into the artefact from the start by writing two dates on every sheet, the date drawn and the date due for review, and treat the review as a small fixed ritual rather than an open-ended project. A practical cycle has three speeds. Annually, on a memorable date, many households use the clock change or a national preparedness week, spend one hour: re-walk the 500-metre ring quickly, re-check the two or three most important data layers for updates, flood map revisions, new facility filings, changed evacuation zones, test the household triggers aloud, and update phone numbers and the out-of-region contact. Seasonally, spend ten minutes at the hinge of your local risk calendar: before storm season, verify drains and gutters clear and the generator or lamps working; before fire season, verify the defensible-space state and the go-bag; before winter, the heating, the carbon monoxide alarm, the ice-storm supplies. Event-driven, update immediately when the world announces a change. The announcements are recognisable: construction uphill or upstream of you, new paving that will shed water faster, a new commercial tenant with cylinders or tankers in the yard, a burned slope above your drainage, a levee or dam inspection making local news, a neighbour's giant tree removed or newly dead, a change in your own household, a baby, a mobility change, a new medical dependency on refrigeration or power. Each of these rewrites some line of the map, and the discipline is to make the edit within the week, while the observation is fresh. Climate drift deserves explicit attention in the annual pass, because baselines are moving in one direction: rainfall intensity records, the length and severity of fire weather seasons, and coastal flood frequencies have shifted measurably within single mortgages, and official maps lag the shift by years. Where your region's trend is documented, published national climate assessments summarise this well, bias your personal margins accordingly: treat the mapped flood zone as optimistic, the fire season as longer than the brochure says, and heat plans as needed one category earlier. Finally, maintain the human layer with the same seriousness as the paper one: rehearse the school-age members yearly, re-walk a route with any new driver, re-brief anyone who joined the household, and after every real activation, a storm, an outage, a near-miss, hold a ten-minute debrief and write what surprised you onto the map. Surprises are the map's error signal, and a household that folds them back in owns a document that gets truer every year instead of staler.

sections.heading: Failure Modes: How Hazard Mapping Goes Wrong
sections.body: The exercise has known pathologies, and naming them is the best inoculation. The first is false precision: treating mapped boundaries as physical walls. The 100-year flood line is a statistical contour drawn through sparse data, not a property of the ground; fires jump highways; plumes wander with the wind. Read every boundary with a margin, one category worse, one street farther, and remember that a third of flood losses occur outside mapped high-risk zones. The second is staleness, covered above but worth restating as a failure: an outdated map is worse than none, because it radiates false authority. The third is spectacle bias: hours spent on the dramatic rare hazard, the volcano, the terror scenario, while the statistically dominant killers at home addresses remain house fire, carbon monoxide, falls, heat, and the car journey during ordinary storms. Let the boring hazards keep their top billing: working smoke and CO alarms, a fire-escape plan, and a decision rule about driving through water outrank most exotic planning. The fourth is analysis as a substitute for action, the comfortable feeling of having researched, which psychologists recognise as a real risk in preparedness work: the map that never becomes triggers, supplies, or a practised route has produced knowledge without capability. Cap the research phase, ship the map, and buy the backflow valve. The fifth is private hoarding of what should be shared. A hazard map improves with neighbours in it and improves them in turn; the evidence from community-based programmes is consistent that street-level familiarity, who has tools, who needs help, who knows first aid, predicts outcomes better than household stockpiles do. Share the non-sensitive layers, the drainage quirks, the exits, the facility bearings, at the level of a street association or a shared document, while keeping genuinely private details, medical dependencies, valuables, your children's rally points, off anything public. The sixth is fear as a product. The purpose of this work is the opposite of anxiety: an unmapped hazardscape generates free-floating dread precisely because it is unbounded, while a mapped one is a finite list of specific, mostly improbable events, each with a rehearsed answer. If the process is producing chronic worry rather than settled confidence, the response is more specificity, not less, finish the trigger table, walk the route, and then put the map away until its review date. And the last failure is forgetting the map's limits on the day itself: real events improvise, and official instructions on the day, evacuation orders, shelter locations, road closures, supersede the pre-drawn plan. The map's job was to make you the kind of household that understands those instructions instantly and moves early; when it has done that, let it be overruled gracefully.

guides.safetyNote: A hazard map is a planning tool, not a prediction. Always follow official warnings and evacuation orders in a real emergency, even when they contradict what your map led you to expect.

guides.title: Building a Household Hazard Risk Assessment
guides.summary: A complete method for identifying, ranking and reducing the hazards that could actually affect your household, from local natural hazards to utility failures and in-home dangers, using the same risk framework professionals use.

sections.heading: Why a Written Assessment Beats General Preparedness
sections.body: Most household preparedness fails in the same way. Someone reads a list, buys a torch, a first aid kit and some tinned food, puts them in a cupboard, and stops. Two years later the batteries have corroded, nobody else in the house knows where the kit is, and the actual event that arrives is a three-day power cut in February for which the household has no heat, no way to charge a phone and no plan for an elderly neighbour. The generic list was not wrong; it was simply not connected to anything specific about this house, these people or this place. A hazard risk assessment fixes that by inverting the order. Instead of starting with supplies, it starts with the question of what can actually happen here, ranks those possibilities by how likely they are and how badly they would hurt, and only then decides where effort and money go. The result is usually surprising. Households living on a floodplain frequently prepare for earthquakes they will never experience; households in earthquake country often have no water stored. The single most common finding of a first assessment is that the biggest realistic risk is something mundane, a kitchen fire, a fall on the stairs, a long power failure, or carbon monoxide from a poorly serviced appliance, rather than the dramatic scenario that preparedness marketing sells. The framework used here is the standard one used in industrial safety, insurance and emergency management, simplified to household scale. Risk is treated as the combination of three things: the likelihood that a hazard occurs, the severity of the consequence if it does, and the vulnerability of the particular household to that consequence. The last is what makes the assessment personal. The same 48-hour power cut is an inconvenience for two fit adults in a well-insulated house, and a potentially fatal event for a person dependent on an oxygen concentrator or on refrigerated insulin. Two houses on the same street can have genuinely different risk profiles. Writing it down matters for three reasons. First, it forces completeness: an unwritten mental list reliably omits the hazards you find unpleasant to think about. Second, it makes the assessment shareable, so that every adult and older child in the household knows the plan rather than one person carrying it in their head, which fails precisely when that person is the casualty. Third, it creates a baseline you can revise. Circumstances change, a new baby, a new job, a relative moving in, a new heating system, and a written assessment can be updated in twenty minutes where a fresh start takes a weekend. Expect the first full pass to take between two and four hours spread over a couple of sessions, and expect the annual review to take under an hour.

sections.heading: The Vocabulary: Hazard, Exposure, Vulnerability, Risk
sections.body: Precision about four words prevents most of the confusion in this work. A hazard is a source of potential harm: floodwater, fire, a gas leak, an icy step, an armed intruder, a heatwave. It exists whether or not anyone is nearby, which is why a bushfire in an uninhabited wilderness is a hazard but produces no risk. Exposure is the presence of people or property in the place and time where a hazard can reach them. A house on a hilltop has essentially zero exposure to river flooding no matter how severe the flood hazard in the valley below. Vulnerability is the degree to which the exposed people or property are susceptible to harm, and it is the factor households most often overlook because it is about them rather than about the world. A single-storey house is more vulnerable to floodwater than a two-storey one because there is nowhere to move possessions or people upward. A household with an infant, a person with limited mobility, or someone whose medication requires refrigeration is more vulnerable to a prolonged power failure. A household where only one adult can drive is more vulnerable to any hazard requiring evacuation. Vulnerability is also the factor most readily reduced: you usually cannot change the hazard, sometimes cannot change the exposure, but can nearly always reduce vulnerability. Risk is the product of these: roughly, likelihood multiplied by consequence, with vulnerability shaping the consequence. Professionals express this in a matrix, and household work is best done with a simple version. Score likelihood from 1 to 5, where 1 means very unlikely in the next ten years, 3 means it will probably happen at some point in ten years, and 5 means it happens most years or is already happening. Score consequence from 1 to 5, where 1 means an annoyance, 3 means significant disruption or expense of a few thousand, and 5 means death, serious injury or loss of the home. Multiply for a risk score from 1 to 25. Anything scoring 12 or above deserves action this month; 6 to 11 deserves a plan this year; below 6 gets noted and reviewed. Two further terms are worth knowing because official sources use them. Residual risk is what remains after your mitigations, and it is never zero; the goal is to make it small and known rather than to eliminate it. Cascading failure is when one event triggers others, which is where households are most often caught out: a storm causes a power cut, the power cut disables the well pump and the electric gate, the loss of water disables the toilet, and a household that prepared only for the storm finds itself defeated by the third-order consequence four days later.

sections.heading: Step One: Establishing Your Local Hazard Baseline
sections.body: The first task is factual rather than imaginative: find out what has actually happened where you live. Local history is the best available predictor, and every region has documented records that most residents have never looked at. National flood mapping services, published by environment agencies in most countries, show the modelled extent of the one-in-100-year and one-in-1000-year flood at street level, and these are usually free and searchable by address. Seismic hazard maps give peak ground acceleration with a stated probability of exceedance, typically 10 per cent in 50 years. Wildfire agencies publish fire danger zones. Meteorological services publish return periods for extreme wind, snow load and temperature. Local authority emergency plans, often available on request, list the hazards the professionals themselves prepare for in your area. Interpret return periods correctly, because they are widely misread. A one-in-100-year flood does not arrive on a schedule; it means a 1 per cent chance in any given year. Over a 30-year mortgage the cumulative probability is not 30 per cent but about 26 per cent, calculated as one minus 0.99 raised to the power 30, which is a substantial risk that many homeowners dismiss because of the reassuring name. Two such floods can occur in consecutive years without anything being unusual. Climate change is also shifting these baselines, so historical return periods increasingly understate current risk for heat, heavy rainfall and coastal surge, and most agencies now publish adjusted projections alongside the historical figures. Supplement the official data with local knowledge, which frequently captures things the maps miss. Neighbours who have lived on the street for decades know which drain backs up, where the road floods before the river does, which corner catches the wind, and how long the power stayed off in the last big storm. Local newspaper archives, now often digitised, give dates and details. If you rent or have recently bought, insurance quotations are an unexpectedly useful signal: insurers price risk professionally, so an unusually high flood or subsidence premium is telling you something concrete. Record the baseline plainly. For each hazard, note whether it has occurred here, when, how severe it was, and what the authoritative source says about frequency. Distinguish clearly between hazards that genuinely apply to your location and those that do not, and be willing to write no meaningful risk beside several of them. A household in central England does not need an earthquake plan; a household in coastal Bangladesh does not need to prioritise blizzards. Discarding irrelevant hazards is not carelessness, it is what frees attention for the ones that will actually arrive. Keep the record of what you rejected and why, though, because the reasoning is what an annual review checks. A hazard dismissed because the nearest river is four kilometres away stays dismissed; a hazard dismissed because a flood defence exists needs revisiting if that defence is downgraded, and utility and planning changes near you are exactly the sort of thing a short yearly check catches while a vague memory of having thought about it does not.

sections.heading: Step Two: The Walk-Through Inventory of the Home Itself
sections.body: Natural hazards get the attention, but the home itself generates the majority of injuries. In most high-income countries, falls are the leading cause of accidental death in the home, dominated by older adults, with residential fires and poisoning following. A structured walk-through, performed room by room with a notebook, finds far more than a general impression does, and it is best done twice: once in daylight and once after dark with only the lighting you actually use. Start outside and work inward. Check the roof line for loose tiles and blocked gutters, the drainage away from the foundations, the condition of steps and handrails, external lighting, and any tree large enough to reach the house if it fell. Note the location of the main water stopcock, the gas shut-off, and the electrical consumer unit, and confirm that each can actually be operated by hand and is not obstructed or seized. Inside, look at every staircase for lighting, handrail security and trip hazards on the treads; at every rug for slip potential; at the bathroom for grab support and hot water temperature; at the kitchen for the position of the extinguisher and fire blanket relative to the cooker, since a blanket stored behind the hob is useless. Attend specifically to the invisible hazards. Carbon monoxide is odourless and kills roughly 400 people a year in the United States and several dozen in the United Kingdom, most from faulty or badly ventilated fuel-burning appliances. Any home with a gas, oil, wood or coal appliance, or an attached garage, needs a carbon monoxide alarm to the current standard, placed at breathing height in sleeping areas and near but not directly above the appliance. Smoke alarms should be on every level and inside each bedroom, interlinked if possible so that one sounding sounds all, and replaced entirely after ten years, since the sensors degrade regardless of battery state. Test monthly using the test button, which checks the electronics and sounder. Also inventory what is stored. Households routinely accumulate hazards without noticing: a partly-used cylinder of butane in a cupboard, several litres of petrol for a mower kept in the garage, cleaning chemicals that produce chlorine gas if mixed, old paint, lithium batteries on charge overnight on a soft surface. Note quantities and locations, because these are what turn a small fire into a fast one. Finally, record the age and last service date of the boiler, the electrical installation, the chimney and any wood-burning appliance. Most jurisdictions recommend annual servicing of combustion appliances and an electrical inspection every ten years for owner-occupied homes and every five for rentals. Write the findings as specific defects with locations rather than as general impressions. Loose second tread on the cellar stairs, no handrail on the left side is actionable; stairs a bit dangerous is not. Photograph anything you may want to compare against later, particularly cracks, damp patches and the condition of flashing and seals, because slow deterioration is invisible from memory and obvious from two photographs a year apart.

sections.heading: Step Three: Profiling the People, Not Just the Property
sections.body: An assessment that stops at the building is half an assessment. The same event produces wildly different outcomes depending on who is in the house, what they depend on, and what they are capable of doing under stress. Work through each member of the household individually and write down four things: their mobility, their dependencies, their capabilities, and their likely location at different times of day. Mobility determines evacuation planning. Ask honestly whether each person can descend stairs unaided in the dark, whether anyone uses a wheelchair, walking frame or crutches, and how long it would take to get everyone out of the building. A realistic figure matters because a house fire typically becomes untenable in two to four minutes once flashover approaches, far faster than in homes of fifty years ago, because modern synthetic furnishings burn hotter and faster. If your honest evacuation time for a sleeping household exceeds three minutes, that number is itself a finding requiring action. Dependencies are the items and services without which someone deteriorates. Prescription medication, and specifically how many days' supply is normally in the house, is the most commonly overlooked. Refrigerated medicines such as insulin, some biologics and certain eye drops fail in a power cut, though insulin in use is generally stable at room temperature for around 28 days, which is worth confirming for the specific product. Powered medical equipment, oxygen concentrators, CPAP machines, nebulisers, powered wheelchairs and stairlifts, all stop when the electricity does, and each needs a specific answer rather than a general one. Note also dependence on a car, on a single earner's income, on a mobile network for care alarms, and on someone outside the household who provides regular care. Capabilities are what the household can do. Who can drive, who can swim, who holds a current first aid certificate, who can shut off the gas and water, who can operate the generator, who speaks the local language fluently. Concentration of capability in one person is a vulnerability in itself; if only one adult knows how to isolate the electricity, the plan fails whenever that adult is absent or injured. Spreading two or three critical skills across at least two people is often the cheapest single improvement available. Finally, map the household's time patterns. Where is everyone at 3 a.m., at 10 a.m. on a weekday, and at 6 p.m.? Children at school and adults at work mean that a daytime event separates the household, which changes the plan entirely: you need agreed meeting points and an out-of-area contact whom everyone can call, because local networks congest first and a distant relative can act as a message relay. Do not forget pets and livestock, which have both needs and, in an evacuation, a documented tendency to make people delay or return into danger for them.

sections.heading: Step Four: Scoring the Risks and Building the Matrix
sections.body: With hazards listed, the property surveyed and the people profiled, the assessment becomes a ranking exercise. The purpose of scoring is not false precision; the numbers are rough by nature and two reasonable people may score the same hazard differently by a point. The purpose is forced comparison. Without a common scale, attention drifts to whatever was most recently in the news, and the household ends up prepared for the vivid rather than the probable. Use a five-by-five matrix. On the likelihood axis, define the levels concretely before scoring anything: 1 for events with no plausible mechanism here, 2 for perhaps once in a lifetime, 3 for once in ten years, 4 for once every few years, 5 for annual or more often. On the consequence axis, define 1 as inconvenience under a day and under a hundred in cost, 2 as a few days of disruption, 3 as significant harm, injury requiring treatment or costs in the low thousands, 4 as severe injury, uninhabitable home or major financial loss, and 5 as fatality or total loss. Score consequence for your household with its actual vulnerabilities, not for a hypothetical average one. Multiply the two for a score from 1 to 25. A worked example clarifies the process. A suburban household considers a 24-hour power cut: likelihood 4, since it has happened twice in six years, and consequence 2, an ordinary inconvenience since they have gas cooking and warm bedding, giving a score of 8. The same household considers a kitchen fire: likelihood 2, but consequence 5, giving 10. It considers a river flood: the map places them outside the 1000-year outline, so likelihood 1 and score 5 or less regardless of consequence. And it considers a fall on the unlit cellar stairs by a 78-year-old resident: likelihood 4 and consequence 4, giving 16, the highest score on the sheet, and pointing directly at a fifty-pound fix with a light fitting and a second handrail. That is precisely the reordering the exercise exists to produce. Two refinements are worth adding. First, score the likelihood over a stated horizon, normally the next ten years, and write the horizon at the top of the sheet so that later reviews are comparable. Second, mark any hazard whose consequence is 5 for special attention even if its likelihood is low, because a catastrophic outcome deserves mitigation out of proportion to its probability when the mitigation is cheap. A carbon monoxide alarm costs very little against a low-probability, fatal-consequence hazard, and no sensible scoring system should let that trade be missed. Keep the whole matrix on one page. If it runs longer, you are recording detail that will never be read. Score with at least two members of the household present if you can. Disagreement about a score is informative rather than obstructive, because it usually reveals that one person is carrying a piece of local knowledge or a private worry the other did not have, and reconciling the two produces a better number than either would have written alone.

sections.heading: Utility Failure: Power, Water, Heat and Communications
sections.body: Loss of utilities is the most probable serious disruption for most households in developed countries, and it is chronically underrated because short outages are common and harmless, which trains people to assume all outages are. The distinction that matters is duration. Under four hours, nothing much happens. Between four and twenty-four hours, refrigerated food becomes a concern and heating or cooling begins to bite. Beyond twenty-four hours, the cascading failures start, and beyond seventy-two hours a household without a plan is in genuine difficulty. For electricity, work out precisely what stops. Beyond lighting, this typically includes the central heating, since almost all gas and oil boilers need mains power for their pumps and controls, so a gas supply does not by itself keep the house warm. It includes the water supply in any home on a private well or on a pumped system, and in flats above the pressure limit of the mains. It includes electric ovens and induction hobs, refrigeration, cordless phones, internet, powered garage and gate motors, and most modern alarm systems after their backup battery expires. A closed refrigerator holds safe temperature for about four hours, a full freezer for about 48 hours and a half-full one for about 24; food above 5 degrees Celsius for more than four cumulative hours should be discarded rather than gambled with, and a freezer thermometer left in place lets you judge afterwards rather than guess. For water, know where your supply comes from and how long you can go without it. A useful planning figure is four litres per person per day for drinking and basic hygiene, doubled in hot climates or for anyone ill, plus a separate allowance for pets. Store at least three days' worth and ideally two weeks'. Commercially bottled water keeps well beyond its date if stored cool and dark; tap water stored in clean food-grade containers should be rotated every six months. Remember that a loss of water pressure also stops toilets, and that a lined bucket with sawdust or cat litter is the standard low-technology answer. For heat, calculate how fast your home actually cools. A well-insulated modern house may lose only a degree or two Celsius per day in mild weather, while an older uninsulated one can drop toward outside temperature within hours. Concentrating the household in a single small room, closing doors, covering windows at night and using layered clothing and sleeping bags is far more effective than any portable heater, and every unflued combustion heater indoors is a carbon monoxide risk. For communications, keep at least one battery or wind-up radio, note that mobile masts have limited backup power measured in hours, and agree in advance that text messages get through congested networks when voice calls do not.

sections.heading: Fire: The Fastest Hazard in the House
sections.body: Fire deserves separate treatment because it moves faster than any other household hazard and because the time available for escape has fallen dramatically within living memory. Testing by fire research laboratories comparing rooms furnished in the style of the 1970s with modern rooms found that time to flashover, the moment when everything in a room ignites more or less at once and the space becomes instantly unsurvivable, fell from roughly seventeen minutes to under four. The cause is the replacement of natural fibres and solid timber with polyurethane foam, synthetic textiles and engineered board, which release heat far faster and produce dense toxic smoke. Most fire deaths result from smoke inhalation rather than burns, and often before flames reach the victim. The practical consequences are specific. Working smoke alarms roughly halve the risk of dying in a house fire, and they must be sited where smoke will reach them early: on every storey, in the hallway outside sleeping areas and inside bedrooms where people sleep with the door closed. Interlinked alarms, either hard-wired or radio-linked, matter more in larger homes because an alarm in the kitchen sounding alone may not wake someone two floors up. Ionisation sensors respond marginally faster to flaming fires and photoelectric ones to smouldering fires; where only one type is fitted, photoelectric is generally preferred because smouldering upholstery fires at night are the deadliest pattern. Closing bedroom doors at night is a genuinely effective and free intervention, keeping the room tens of degrees cooler and dramatically reducing smoke ingress. Ignition sources should be inventoried honestly. Cooking is the leading cause of household fires almost everywhere, followed by electrical faults and heating appliances. Unattended cooking, chip pans and overloaded extension leads account for a large share. Lithium-ion batteries, particularly in e-bikes, e-scooters and cheap replacement chargers, have become a fast-growing cause; a cell in thermal runaway produces its own oxidiser and cannot be extinguished with a conventional extinguisher, so the mitigation is to charge such batteries away from escape routes, never overnight while sleeping, and never on a soft surface. Equipment should match the plan. A fire blanket by the kitchen door, not behind the hob, handles pan fires; a multi-purpose dry powder or foam extinguisher is a reasonable general choice, but note that using one is only ever appropriate on a small fire with your escape route behind you and after everyone else is leaving. Never throw water on burning oil, which causes explosive steam expansion and a fireball. Plan two escape routes from every room, keep keys for window and door locks in a consistent place all household members know, and keep hallways clear. The single most valuable exercise is to walk the escape route with the household at night with the lights off, because the route that seems obvious in daylight is a different proposition in darkness and smoke.

sections.heading: Water: Flood, Leak and Contamination
sections.body: Water damages homes on three quite different timescales, and a household assessment should treat them separately. External flooding arrives from rivers, from the sea, from surface water when rainfall exceeds drainage capacity, and from groundwater rising through floors. Surface water flooding is the type most people fail to anticipate, because it can happen well away from any river whenever intense rainfall meets saturated ground or blocked drains, and it is increasing as rainfall intensity rises. Check whether your property sits at a local low point, whether the ground slopes toward the building, and whether the drains serving your street have a history of backing up. Depth matters enormously to consequence. Fifteen centimetres of water in a ground floor destroys flooring, skirting, plasterboard to a height well above the water line by wicking, and any appliance with a motor near the floor, and typically means several months out of the property while it dries and is repaired. A metre of water reaches sockets and consumer units. Floodwater is also contaminated, commonly with sewage, so the clean-up is a health matter and not merely a drying exercise. Only 15 centimetres of moving water can knock an adult off their feet and 30 can float most cars, which is why the standing advice never to drive or walk through floodwater is not excessive caution. Internal water failures are far more likely than floods for most households and are the largest category of home insurance claim in many countries. Burst pipes in a cold snap, failed washing machine hoses, leaking shower trays and overflowing baths cause enormous cumulative damage. The cheap mitigations are knowing where the internal stop tap is and confirming it turns, insulating pipes in unheated spaces, replacing rubber appliance hoses with braided stainless ones every five years, and leaving heating on a low setting rather than fully off when a house is empty in freezing weather. A leak detector under the washing machine or by the boiler costs very little. Contamination is the third pathway. A boil-water notice, a burst main drawing in dirt, or floodwater entering a private well all make a supply unsafe. Boiling for one minute at a rolling boil, or three minutes above 2,000 metres altitude, kills bacteria, viruses and protozoa including Cryptosporidium and Giardia, and is the most reliable household method. Chemical disinfection with unscented household bleach at roughly two drops of 5 to 6 per cent sodium hypochlorite per litre, left 30 minutes, is a fallback that does not reliably kill Cryptosporidium. Neither boiling nor bleach removes chemical contamination, heavy metals or fuel, so a supply suspected of chemical pollution must simply not be used. Record for your own property which of these three pathways is realistic, at what depth, and what the first sign would be. For most households the honest answer is that external flooding is unlikely, internal escape of water is close to certain over a couple of decades, and a temporary contamination notice is a once-a-decade nuisance. That ordering should drive where the money goes.

sections.heading: Weather Extremes: Heat, Cold and Wind
sections.body: Extreme temperature kills more people in most temperate countries than any dramatic natural disaster, and it does so quietly, mostly among the old, the isolated and the chronically ill. The 2003 European heatwave is estimated to have caused around 70,000 excess deaths, and heatwaves in 2022 and subsequent years have repeatedly produced tens of thousands more. Because these deaths are dispersed and attributed to cardiac and respiratory causes, households consistently underrate heat as a hazard. Heat risk depends on the combination of temperature and humidity, because the body sheds heat mainly by evaporating sweat and high humidity blocks that route. Wet-bulb temperature captures this, and sustained wet-bulb readings above about 35 degrees Celsius are survivable for only a few hours even by a healthy person at rest in shade with water, though serious harm begins far below that threshold for vulnerable people. Practical mitigation is unglamorous: identify the coolest room in the house, usually north-facing on the ground floor; shade windows from the outside, which is several times more effective than internal blinds; ventilate at night and close up during the day when outside is hotter than inside; use fans only while air temperature is below about 35 degrees, since above that a fan blows hot air over the skin and can increase heat gain; and identify in advance a public building with air conditioning. Note which household medications, including diuretics, beta-blockers, antipsychotics and anticholinergics, impair heat tolerance. Cold risk is the mirror image and is dominated by the loss of heating during a power failure. Indoor temperatures below about 18 degrees Celsius begin to raise blood pressure and respiratory risk, and below 12 the cardiovascular strain becomes significant for older people. Hypothermia indoors is a real and under-recognised event among frail elderly residents. Plan for a single warm room, insulation of that room's windows and doors, layered dry clothing including a hat, hot drinks and food, and a way to detect that someone living alone has become too cold, which usually means a daily check by a named person. Wind and storm risk is more about the building envelope. Note trees within falling distance, the condition of roof coverings and ridge tiles, fences and outbuildings, and anything on a balcony or in a garden that becomes a projectile above about 20 metres per second. Bring loose items in before a forecast storm rather than during it, park vehicles away from trees, and identify the room with fewest windows and the shortest roof span as the place to shelter. Where lightning is a hazard, the rule is simple: when thunder follows the flash by 30 seconds or less, go indoors and stay in for 30 minutes after the last thunder. For all three, the forecast is the trigger. Modern meteorological warnings give named colour or numbered levels with defined meanings, and a household that has written down in advance what it will do at each level has converted a vague sense of bad weather coming into a checklist.

sections.heading: Medical Emergencies, Security and Other Human Hazards
sections.body: Not every household hazard comes from weather or machinery. The most statistically likely serious event in an average home over a decade is a medical emergency affecting one of its occupants, and very few households have thought about it as a planning problem rather than as a matter of calling for help and hoping. The planning questions are concrete. Does anyone know the address well enough to give it clearly under stress, including a postcode or what3words-style reference for an ambiguous rural property? Can an ambulance crew get in if the only conscious occupant cannot open the door, and is a key safe fitted with the code known to a relative? Is there a written list of each person's conditions, medications with doses, allergies and doctor, kept where a paramedic would find it, conventionally on the refrigerator door? Cardiac arrest is the case where household preparation changes outcomes most sharply. Survival falls by roughly 7 to 10 percentage points for every minute without cardiopulmonary resuscitation and defibrillation, so bystander action in the first four minutes matters more than anything the ambulance service can do afterwards. Knowing the location of the nearest public access defibrillator, and having at least two adults in the household trained in CPR, is a high-value, low-cost mitigation that scores well on any honest matrix. Choking, severe bleeding and anaphylaxis are the other three where minutes decide the outcome and simple training pays. Security hazards should be assessed with the same discipline and without either paranoia or denial. Look at the actual pattern of crime in your immediate area rather than at national reporting, which is usually available from police open data. The overwhelming majority of residential burglaries are opportunistic and defeated by ordinary measures: good locks on doors and accessible windows, lighting, removing the cover of high fences and unlit alleyways, not leaving keys visible near a letterbox, and simply making the property look occupied. Consider also the hazard of being present during a break-in and agree in advance that property is not worth confrontation. Two further human hazards belong on the list because they are common and rarely written down. The first is scam and fraud exposure, particularly for older household members, where the practical mitigation is an agreed rule that no financial decision is made during an unexpected phone call and a named person is always consulted first. The second is the risk that a household member becomes the emergency: a mental health crisis, a fall while alone, or a person who does not return when expected. Agree what triggers concern, who checks, and what the escalation is, because the alternative is a household paralysed by uncertainty about whether it is overreacting. Agreeing the rule while everyone is calm also removes the embarrassment that stops people acting, since nobody has to decide in the moment whether raising the alarm makes them look foolish.

sections.heading: Choosing Responses: Eliminate, Reduce, Transfer, Accept
sections.body: Once risks are ranked, each one needs a decision, and there are only four things you can do with a risk. You can eliminate the hazard, reduce the likelihood or the consequence, transfer the financial consequence to someone else, or accept it consciously. Every entry on the matrix should end up labelled with one of these, and writing accepted beside a low-scoring risk is a legitimate and valuable outcome, quite different from failing to notice it. Elimination is the strongest control and is available more often than people expect. Removing the stored petrol can from an attached garage eliminates a hazard rather than managing it. Replacing an unflued paraffin heater with an electric one eliminates a carbon monoxide source. Taking down a diseased tree within falling distance of the bedroom eliminates the exposure. Professional safety practice ranks controls in a hierarchy for a reason: elimination and substitution do not depend on anyone behaving correctly under stress, whereas procedures and warnings do, and human performance degrades exactly when it is needed. Prefer the fix that works while everyone is asleep. Reduction splits into reducing likelihood and reducing consequence, and both deserve attention because they act at different points. Servicing the boiler annually reduces the likelihood of a carbon monoxide release; the alarm reduces the consequence if one happens anyway. Managing vegetation reduces the likelihood of a wildfire reaching the house; non-combustible cladding and ember-proof vents reduce the consequence. A well-built plan usually has one measure of each kind for every high-scoring hazard, because likelihood reduction alone leaves you with no defence on the day it fails. Transfer means insurance, and it is worth treating analytically rather than as a bill. Read what is actually covered, especially the exclusions for gradual leaks, for flood if you are in a mapped zone, and for accidental damage. Check whether the sum insured reflects the genuine rebuild cost rather than market value, and whether contents cover includes a realistic figure, since most households substantially underinsure. Photograph or video every room and store the record off-site or in cloud storage; claims are settled far faster with evidence. Note that insurance transfers money, never the disruption, so it is a complement to mitigation and not a substitute. Acceptance is the honest label for risks whose mitigation costs more than the expected loss, and for those you simply cannot address. A household that cannot afford flood resilience measures this year should record that, note the trigger that would change the decision, and move on rather than letting an unresolved item quietly discredit the whole plan. A useful discipline when choosing among competing measures is to divide the reduction in risk score by the cost in money and effort. A second stair handrail at modest cost that drops a 16 to a 6 beats an expensive generator that drops an 8 to a 6, and doing that arithmetic out loud protects the budget from whatever felt most frightening on the day the assessment was written.

sections.heading: Turning the Assessment Into Supplies and Documents
sections.body: Supplies come last, and they come from the matrix rather than from a generic list. A household whose top risks are a 72-hour winter power cut and a kitchen fire needs warmth, light, communications and an extinguisher, not a water filter and a machete. Work down the ranked list and ask, for each high-scoring hazard, what a person will actually reach for in the first hour, the first day and the first three days. Then buy only those things, store them where the plan says they will be needed, and tell everyone where they are. The most commonly neglected part is documents, which cost nothing and matter enormously afterwards. Insurance claims, temporary accommodation, replacement prescriptions, school enrolment and access to money all depend on paperwork that may be inside the damaged building. Keep a scanned set in encrypted cloud storage and a physical copy in a grab bag or with a relative. Test that you can actually open the cloud copy from a phone without your usual computer, because an account requiring a code from a device that burned is not a backup. The list below is a starting set to be edited against your own matrix, not a shopping list to be bought entire. Rotate consumables on a fixed date each year, and note that most equipment failures found during real events are flat batteries and expired items rather than missing kit.
ingredients: Water: four litres per person per day for at least three days, in food-grade containers or commercially bottled, stored cool and dark; plus a means of treatment, either a rolling boil or unscented 5 to 6 per cent sodium hypochlorite bleach with a measuring dropper.
Light: one headtorch per person, LED, with spare alkaline or lithium cells stored separately from the device to prevent corrosion; candles are a fire hazard and a poor substitute.

Communications: a battery or wind-up radio capable of receiving national emergency broadcasts, a power bank of at least 10,000 milliamp-hours per phone, and the written phone numbers of an out-of-area contact, since nobody memorises numbers any more.
Warmth: sleeping bags or extra blankets rated for the coldest indoor temperature you calculated, hats and thermal layers, and a plan for a single heated room.

Food: three to fourteen days of items that need no cooking and no refrigeration, chosen for what the household will actually eat, plus a manual can opener and any specialist infant or medical nutrition.
Medical: a first aid kit sized to the household, a two-week buffer of every regular prescription where the prescriber permits it, and a written list of conditions, doses and allergies.
Fire and utility control: a fire blanket by the kitchen exit, an appropriate extinguisher, and the correct tools kept beside the gas, water and electrical isolation points.

Documents: identification, insurance policies with claim numbers, property deeds or tenancy agreement, medical summaries, bank details and photographs of every room, held both digitally off-site and as a physical copy.

sections.heading: Shelter in Place or Leave: Deciding Before the Day
sections.body: Every hazard on the matrix resolves eventually into one of two responses: stay put and make the building safe, or leave and go somewhere else. Getting this decision wrong is the commonest way a survivable event becomes a fatal one, and the reason is that the decision is usually made under time pressure by people who have never considered it. Deciding in advance, hazard by hazard, converts a judgement call into a recognition. The general rule is that you shelter when the danger is outside and the building protects you, and you leave when the danger is inside the building or is coming for the building itself. Shelter is the right answer for most storms, for a chemical release outdoors, where you close windows, shut off ventilation and go to an interior room on a higher floor since many industrial gases are denser than air, and for extreme cold. Leaving is the right answer for fire, for gas leaks, for structural damage, for wildfire approaching, and for flooding where the water is rising and the building has no safe upper storey. For flooding specifically, the decision must be made early, because once roads are cut the choice disappears and rescue may take days. Write a trigger for each. A trigger is an observable condition, not a feeling: the official warning reaches a stated level, the water reaches the second step of the drive, the smoke alarm sounds and is not a burnt toast false alarm, the carbon monoxide alarm sounds at all, the wind forecast exceeds a stated speed. Triggers work because they remove the negotiation with yourself that otherwise consumes the available time. Pair each trigger with an action and a person responsible. Plan the leaving in detail, because that is where failures cluster. Decide the primary and secondary routes, and remember that the primary road is the one everyone else will also take. Decide the destination: a named relative or friend, ideally in a different direction from the likely hazard and far enough away not to be affected by the same event, plus an official reception centre as a fallback. Keep vehicles above half a tank of fuel or half charge during any hazard season, since fuel stations need electricity to pump. Decide who collects the children and who collects the person who cannot drive, and agree that only one person does each so nobody makes a second dangerous journey. Agree a meeting point outside the property and a second one outside the immediate area. Finally, decide in advance what you will not go back for, and say it out loud, because the pull to return for possessions and pets kills people every year. Where pets are concerned, the workable answer is preparation rather than prohibition: carriers stored by the exit, leads on a hook by the door, and a note of which accommodation and reception centres accept animals, so that taking them out is quick and the temptation to go back does not arise.

sections.heading: Keeping the Assessment Alive: Drills, Review and Handover
sections.body: An assessment written once and filed is a document, not a capability. What converts one into the other is a small amount of recurring maintenance and at least one honest rehearsal, because plans that have never been executed contain errors that only execution reveals: the escape window painted shut, the key safe whose code nobody remembers, the torch with corroded cells, the meeting point that turns out to be on the far side of the road everyone must cross. Rehearsal need not be elaborate. A fire escape drill, done once with everyone present, at night, with the lights off, from bedrooms, typically takes four minutes and finds two or three problems. A tabletop walk-through, in which one person reads out a scenario and everyone says what they would do, costs twenty minutes and finds the gaps in the decision-making rather than the physical layout. Doing one of each per year is a realistic standard for an ordinary household, and doing the fire drill within a month of any change to sleeping arrangements is worth the small nuisance. Handover deserves particular attention, because most household plans live in one person's head. Everyone capable of understanding it should know where the assessment is kept, where the supplies are, how to isolate gas, water and electricity, the out-of-area contact number, and the meeting points. Children can hold more of this than adults expect if it is taught calmly. Someone outside the household, typically a nearby relative or a trusted neighbour, should know enough to act if the household is unreachable.
